**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  1. Preserve linear-time removal when matching aliases**

For statements with many unused members, this linear search runs once per CST alias, making F401 fix generation quadratic instead of using the previous counted hash-map lookup. This also affects ordinary unaliased imports because `fix_by_removing_imports` now always uses this helper. An isolated benchmark of this loop with 32,000 source-ordered members performed 256 million string comparisons, taking approximately 0.7 seconds versus 7 milliseconds for a counted map. Use a counted `FxHashMap` keyed by `(member_name, alias)` to preserve duplicate handling without introducing this large-statement performance regression.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

<!-- codex-code-review-finding:v1 -->

> Why can't we rely on the latter for generic cases as well?

Having the heuristic within the solver allows it to be applied per type variable, rather than looking at the entire RHS expression. For example, the heuristic allows us to preserve graduality in second element of the tuple below, despite the first element preventing the tuples themselves from being mutually assignable.

```py
def _(a: tuple[int, str]):
    x: tuple[object, Any] = a
    reveal_type(x)  # revealed: tuple[int, str]

def f[T, U](x: T, y: U) -> tuple[T, U]:
    return (x, y)

def _(a: int, b: str):
    x: tuple[object, Any] = f(a, b)
    reveal_type(x)  # revealed: tuple[int, Any]
```

It also applies between the elements of a `list` and a `Sequence`, for example:

```py
def _(a: list[int]):
    x: Sequence[Any] = a
    reveal_type(x)  # revealed: list[int]

def _(a: int):
    x: Sequence[Any] = list((a,))
    reveal_type(x)  # revealed: list[Any]
```

> But it doesn't seem clear that there's a principled reason why generic cases should behave differently from non-generic ones in this respect.

Yeah, this is a good point. It's not clear to me what sources of type context this should apply to. It should be quite easy to restrict the preference to specific `TypeContextKind`s though, if we want to change this.

body:
This makes sense. What remains unclear to me is why this preference needs to be implemented inside generic inference via type context, rather than allowing assignment handling to take care of it, which is how it works for non-generic cases. E.g. for `x: int = bare_name_typed_as_any`, we still infer the expression `bare_name_typed_as_any` itself as `Any`, and then we have code in `TypeInferenceBuilder::add_declaration_with_binding` that does the mutual-assignability check and decides to prefer the declared type over the inferred type. Why can't we rely on the latter for generic cases as well?

One notable difference between the two is that our non-generic handling applies only to _immediate_ type context, it doesn't apply to e.g. `x: int` and then a later `x = typed_as_any`. I tried making it apply to all later assignments and the results didn't look good. But it doesn't seem clear that there's a principled reason why generic cases should behave differently from non-generic ones in this respect.

I don't think we ever need source text overrides for stubs

> I think this calls into question the desirability of the mutually-assignable heuristic implemented in this PR for generic inference. I'm not sure if there are cases where that heuristic gives clearly better results, but this case makes me wonder if it was partly motivated by increased removal of unsound-* diagnostics in the ecosystem, even in some cases where those diagnostics are actually correct and desirable.

Hmm.. that was certainly not the motivation. The idea behind using the heuristic here was to preserve inference behavior that we already have on main with invariant types:

```py
def _(x: int, y: Any):
    xs: list[Any] = reveal_type([x])  # revealed: list[Any]
    ys: list[int] = reveal_type([y])  # revealed: list[int]
```

Naively solving the constraints here without declared type preference would produce `int | Any` in both cases. In the first case, this is undesirable because we restrict the graduality that was explicitly declared by the user. In the second case, this also seems undesirable because we introduce graduality despite the user declaring a concrete element type.

In the legacy solver, this heuristic is framed as a blanket preference of the declared type in invariant position. However, it specifically targets this issue with dynamic types (i.e., to prefer `list[Any]` as declared over `list[int | Any]`, both of which are valid solutions). In non-invariant position (e.g., `Sequence[Any]`), the same logic would seem to apply, but a blanket preference of the declared type leads to obvious issues (we don't want `x: object = identity(1)` to infer `object`, for example). I played with a lot of different ideas for how to handle this but decided that applying the mutual-assignability heuristic per-typevar makes a lot of sense here, while also being consistent with how we handle declared types in general in annotated assignments.

The `unsound-*` false negatives does seem like an issue. It is worth noting though that the `ys` example above should also arguably produce an `unsound-assignment-diagnostic`. Perhaps the solution here is just to check the original argument types against the chosen specialization, rather than change the solution we infer?

Going to leave this as a follow up and restore the original guard here for now, this PR shouldn't really be touching the legacy path.

Filed https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/4951 to track this.

We actually shouldn't need these disjointness filters anymore! However, removing them exposed some minor regressions that I don't want to fix in this PR, so I'll leave that for a follow up. In the meantime, I added a fast-path exact membership check to the disjointness checker that should mitigate this issue (a generalized version of your suggestion), though it doesn't seem to affect the Pydantic regression.

Filed https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/4952 to track this.
I added a test and TODO comment for this idea, it's a little tricky because with `x: A | B = ...` we narrow the call to `A` and `B` individually, so don't have access to the full union.

The fact that this line _doesn't_ emit an `unsound-assignment` anymore in this PR seems undesirable to me -- this seems like exactly a case that `unsound-assignment` was intended to catch.

In the ecosystem report on this PR, scikit-build-core returns `frozenset(tomllib.load(f)["tool"]["scikit-build"][name]["known-wheels"])` from a function annotated `-> frozenset[str]`. Main warns about returning `frozenset[Unknown]` via `unsound-return-statement`. That warning is correct: the return really is silently and unsoundly asserting that unknown gradually-typed data is strings. This PR silences that desirable warning. [scikit-build-core example](https://github.com/scikit-build/scikit-build-core/blob/f908b68a4efc437fce35841e91553934fba4402a/src/scikit_build_core/builder/_known_wheels.py#L25-L28)

This is basically the flip side of [ty#4294](https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/4294). There, `return frozenset()` is sound for a function annotated `-> frozenset[CodeType]` because an empty immutable set can never contain an element of the wrong type. Using the return annotation to infer the element type removes a false positive from `unsound-return-statement`.

This isn't (just) https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/4536. Even in cases where we do retain the gradual evidence (`frozenset(items)` where `items: Iterable[Any]`), we now allow an expected return type of `frozenset[str]` to override the `Any` (because they are mutually assignable), and this silences `unsound-return-statement`.

I think this calls into question the desirability of the mutually-assignable heuristic implemented in this PR for generic inference. I'm not sure if there are cases where that heuristic gives clearly better results, but this case makes me wonder if it was partly motivated by increased removal of `unsound-*` diagnostics in the ecosystem, even in some cases where those diagnostics are actually correct and desirable.

I don't think false negatives on `unsound-*` is a blocker, given those rules aren't even enabled by default, so we could sort this out as a follow-up. But I think it does deserve a follow-up tracking issue, and maybe even a test with TODO in `assignment/unsound.md`.

+//! Computes source edits for Python file renames.
+//!
+//! ## Overview
+//!
+//! [`will_rename_files`] maps filesystem renames to module names, then computes edits for import
+//! statements and references in indexed project files. It does not move files, discover package
+//! contents, validate the filesystem operation, or normalize the returned edits.
+//!
+//! EXAMPLE:
+//!
+//! When `pkg/old.py` is renamed to `pkg/new.py`, the following code:
+//!
+//! ```python
+//! from pkg import old
+//! print(old.C)
+//! ```
+//!
+//! is updated like so:
+//!
+//! ```python
+//! from pkg import new
+//! print(new.C)
+//! ```
+//!
+//! [`will_rename_files`] computes edits over all files in parallel using [`edits_for_file`]. That
+//! in turn computes edits for a single file in two distinct AST passes: [`ImportStatementVisitor`]
+//! visits import statements and computes edits for them, then [`ModuleReferenceVisitor`] visits
+//! all references to imported modules and computes edits for those references. Those two sets of
+//! edits are combined to produce the final result.
+//!
+//! ## Terminology
+//!
+//! Below is the anatomy of the two types of import statement.
+//!
+//! A "plain" import statement:
+//!
+//! ```text
+//!              Alias
+//!        +---------------+
+//! import pkg.old as stable
+//!        |          |
+//!        |          explicit alias
+//!        imported name
+//! ```
+//!
+//! and an "import-from" statement:
+//!
+//! ```text
+//!                       Alias
+//!                   +-----------+
+//! from ..pkg import old as stable
+//!      | |            |      |
+//!      | module name  |      explicit alias
+//!      |              imported name
+//!      |
+//!      import level
+//! ```
+//!
+//! From there, we can layer on a few additional terms.
+//!
+//! | Term | Meaning | Example |
+//! | --- | --- | --- |
+//! | Bound name | A name introduced by an import. | `stable` in both diagrams. |
+//! | Module reference | The use of a module in an expression. | `old` in `old.C`; `pkg.old` in `pkg.old.C`. |
+//! | Re-export | A name that a module imports from elsewhere and makes available through its own namespace. | `facade.py`: `from pkg import old`; elsewhere: `from facade import old`. |
+//! | Imported name edit | Replacement of an imported name. | `import old` → `import new`, `import pkg.old` → `import pkg.new` |
+//! | Module name edit | Replacement of the module name in an import-from statement. | `from old import C` → `from new import C`. |
+//! | Bound name change | Change to a bound name caused by an imported name edit. | `old` → `new`; no bound name change for an explicit alias like `as stable`. |
+//! | Reference edit | Replacement at a module reference. | `old.C` → `new.C`. |
+//! | Source edit | Source range and replacement text. | Range of `old`, replacement `new`. |
+//!
+//! The above terms are used consistently throughout this module.
+
+use crate::RangedValue;
+use rayon::prelude::*;
+use ruff_db::files::{File, FileRange};
+use ruff_db::source::source_text;
+use ruff_db::system::{SystemPath, SystemPathBuf};
+use ruff_python_ast::visitor::source_order::{SourceOrderVisitor, TraversalSignal};
+use ruff_python_ast::{self as ast, AnyNodeRef};
+use ruff_python_trivia::NameMatcher;
+use ruff_text_size::{Ranged, TextRange};
+use rustc_hash::{FxHashMap, FxHashSet};
+use ty_module_resolver::{
+    Module, ModuleName, ModuleResolveMode, ResolverEnvironment, ResolverFile, file_to_module,
+    resolve_module_confident, resolve_real_module_confident, search_paths,
+};
+use ty_project::{Db, parallel::ParallelIteratorExt};
+use ty_python_core::definition::{Definition, DefinitionKind};
+use ty_python_semantic::types::Type;
+use ty_python_semantic::{DefinitionResolution, HasType, SemanticModel};
+
+/// Computes source edits for a batch of Python file renames.
+///
+/// The following types of rename request are not yet supported:
+///
+/// - A request that renames a directory
+/// - A request that changes a module parent (e.g., renaming `a.old` to `b.new` or `new`)
+/// - A request that renames an `__init__.py` or `__init__.pyi` file
+/// - A request that changes the extension of a module (e.g., from `.py` to `.pyi`)
+///
+/// When a rename batch contains both supported and unsupported requests, the unsupported requests
+/// are skipped while the supported ones produce edits as normal.
+///
+/// The returned edits refer to the original files and source ranges. The caller must sort the edits
+/// and handle duplicates and overlaps before applying them.
+///
+/// ## Unsupported edits
+///
+/// Even for supported renames, some occurrences are not updated:
+///
+/// - Name references supplied by star imports, such as `from pkg import *`.
+/// - Names in `global` and `nonlocal` declarations, and references whose resolution crosses those
+///   declarations.
+/// - Names and attributes being assigned to or deleted. Receiver expressions can still be updated.
+/// - Names in ordinary strings, including `__all__` entries and dynamic imports (although module
+///   references in string annotations are supported).
+///
+/// Other edits may still be returned, so an import can be updated while a reference to its old
+/// name remains unchanged.
+///
+/// Additionally, an ambiguous imported name is left unchanged even when other names in the same
+/// import-from statement are updated. For example, suppose we rename `old.py` to `new.py` and
+/// `other.py` to `another.py`:
+///
+/// ```python
+/// # facade.py
+/// import old
+/// import other
+/// if flag:
+///     old = 0
+///
+/// # use.py
+/// from facade import other, old
+/// ```
+///
+/// In the import from `facade`, `old` may or may not refer to the renamed module, so it is left
+/// unchanged. The import becomes `from facade import another, old`.
+fn will_rename_files(db: &dyn Db, renames: &[FileRename]) -> Vec<FileRenameEdit> {
+    let files: Vec<_> = db.project().files(db).iter().collect();
+    let module_name_changes = ModuleNameChanges::new(db, renames);
+    if module_name_changes.is_empty() {
+        return Vec::new();
+    }
+
+    files
+        .into_par_iter()
+        .map_with_db(db, |db, file| {
+            edits_for_file(db, file, &module_name_changes)
+        })
+        .flatten()
+        .collect()
+}
+
+/// One Python file rename in a batch.
+struct FileRename {
+    /// The source file before the rename.
+    file: File,
+    /// The destination path, which need not exist yet.
+    new_path: SystemPathBuf,
+}
+
+/// A replacement and the file range containing it.
+type FileRenameEdit = RangedValue<String>;
+
+/// Maps old module names to new module names for supported file renames.
+struct ModuleNameChanges<'db> {
+    // A map from old module name to new module name for supported rename operations.
+    module_renames: FxHashMap<&'db ModuleName, ModuleName>,
+    // The module basename for each key in `module_renames` (e.g., `old` in `pkg.old`).
+    old_module_basenames: FxHashSet<&'db str>,
+    // Used to check whether a source file may contain an old module basename.
+    old_module_basename_matchers: Vec<NameMatcher<'db>>,
+}
+
+impl<'db> ModuleNameChanges<'db> {
+    fn new(db: &'db dyn Db, renames: &[FileRename]) -> Self {
+        let module_renames: FxHashMap<_, _> = renames
+            .iter()
+            .filter_map(|rename| module_rename(db, rename))
+            .filter(|(old_module_name, new_module_name)| *old_module_name != new_module_name)
+            .collect();
+        let old_module_basenames: FxHashSet<&'db str> = module_renames
+            .keys()
+            .map(|&module_name| module_name.last_component())
+            .collect();
+        let old_module_basename_matchers = old_module_basenames
+            .iter()
+            .map(|&basename| NameMatcher::new(basename))
+            .collect();
+        Self {
+            module_renames,
+            old_module_basenames,
+            old_module_basename_matchers,
+        }
+    }
+
+    fn is_empty(&self) -> bool {
+        self.module_renames.is_empty()
+    }
+
+    fn new_module_name(&self, old_module_name: &ModuleName) -> Option<&ModuleName> {
+        self.module_renames.get(old_module_name)
+    }
+
+    fn is_old_module_basename(&self, name: &str) -> bool {
+        self.old_module_basenames.contains(name)
+    }
+
+    /// Returns whether the source may need edits for these module name changes.
+    fn may_affect_source(&self, source: &str) -> bool {
+        self.old_module_basename_matchers
+            .iter()
+            .any(|matcher| matcher.may_match(source))
+    }
+}
+
+/// Computes edits for one candidate file in two AST passes.
+///
+/// 1. [`ImportStatementVisitor`] traverses import statements in the AST to compute edits to those
+///    statements specifically, and to record bound name changes.
+/// 2. [`ModuleReferenceVisitor`] traverses many different AST nodes to computes edits to each
+///    reference to an imported module. Reaching definitions determine which module references need
+///    updating after a bound name change.
+///
+/// Computing import statement edits first lets us base reference edits on the bound name changes,
+/// accounting for explicit aliases and re-exports. A rejected imported name edit leaves its
+/// bound name unchanged.
+fn edits_for_file(
+    db: &dyn Db,
+    file: File,
+    module_name_changes: &ModuleNameChanges<'_>,
+) -> Vec<FileRenameEdit> {
+    let program_file = db.program_file(file);
+    let source = source_text(db, file);
+    if !module_name_changes.may_affect_source(&source) {
+        return Vec::new();
+    }
+
+    let parsed_module = ruff_db::parsed::parsed_module(db, program_file.python_file(db)).load(db);
+    let root = AnyNodeRef::from(parsed_module.syntax());
+    let model = SemanticModel::new(db, program_file);
+    let mut bound_name_change_cache = BoundNameChangeCache::new(module_name_changes);
+
+    let import_statement_changes = {
+        let mut import_statement_visitor =
+            ImportStatementVisitor::new(db, &model, &mut bound_name_change_cache);
+        root.visit_source_order(&mut import_statement_visitor);
+        import_statement_visitor.changes
+    };
+
+    let mut module_reference_visitor = ModuleReferenceVisitor::new(
+        db,
+        &model,
+        &source,
+        &import_statement_changes.bound_name_changes,
+        &mut bound_name_change_cache,
+    );
+    root.visit_source_order(&mut module_reference_visitor);
+
+    let mut edits = import_statement_changes.edits;
+    edits.extend(module_reference_visitor.edits);
+    edits
+}
+
+/// Computes imported name and module name edits, and records bound name changes.

+/// ```python

+///
+/// ```python
+/// import pkg.new
+/// ```

+/// and
+///
+/// ```python
+/// from pkg.old import C
+/// ```
+///
+/// to
+///
+/// ```python
+/// from pkg.new import C

+/// we never introduce an explicit alias where there wasn't one before, or change the import level in
+/// a relative import.

+/// sharing a [`BoundNameChangeCache`] across import statements.

+    db: &'db dyn Db,
+    editor: ImportStatementEditor<'a, 'db>,
+    bound_name_change_cache: &'a mut BoundNameChangeCache<'db>,
+    changes: ImportStatementChanges<'db>,
+}

+impl<'a, 'db> ImportStatementVisitor<'a, 'db> {
+    fn new(
+        db: &'db dyn Db,
+        model: &'a SemanticModel<'db>,
+        bound_name_change_cache: &'a mut BoundNameChangeCache<'db>,
+    ) -> Self {
+        Self {
+            db,
+            editor: ImportStatementEditor::new(model, bound_name_change_cache.module_name_changes),
+            bound_name_change_cache,
+            changes: ImportStatementChanges::default(),
+        }
+    }
+}

+impl<'a> SourceOrderVisitor<'a> for ImportStatementVisitor<'a, '_> {
+    fn enter_node(&mut self, node: AnyNodeRef<'a>) -> TraversalSignal {

+            AnyNodeRef::StmtImport(statement) => self.editor.edit_plain_import(statement),
+            AnyNodeRef::StmtImportFrom(statement) => self.editor.edit_import_from(
+                statement,
+                &mut ModuleMemberNameAnalyzer::new(self.db, self.bound_name_change_cache),
+            ),
+            _ => return TraversalSignal::Traverse,
+        };

+        if let Some(changes) = changes {
+            self.changes.extend(changes);
+        }

+        // The import statement has been handled, so its descendants
+        // (e.g., aliases) do not need a separate visit.
+        TraversalSignal::Skip
+    }

+    // Plain import statements and import-from statements cannot occur inside expressions.
+    fn visit_expr(&mut self, _expr: &'a ast::Expr) {}
+}

+/// Computes edits and bound name changes for one import statement.
+struct ImportStatementEditor<'a, 'db> {
+    model: &'a SemanticModel<'db>,
+    module_name_changes: &'a ModuleNameChanges<'db>,
+}
+
+impl<'a, 'db> ImportStatementEditor<'a, 'db> {
+    fn new(model: &'a SemanticModel<'db>, module_name_changes: &'a ModuleNameChanges<'db>) -> Self {
+        Self {
+            model,
+            module_name_changes,
+        }
+    }
+
+    /// Computes imported name edits for a plain import statement, such as `import old` to `import new`.
+    ///
+    /// Returns `None` if no source edits or bound name changes are produced.
+    fn edit_plain_import(
+        &self,
+        statement: &ast::StmtImport,
+    ) -> Option<ImportStatementChanges<'db>> {
+        let mut changes = ImportStatementChanges::default();
+        for alias in &statement.names {
+            match self.should_edit_imported_name_for_plain_import(alias) {
+                EditDecision::Yes(new_imported_name) => {
+                    self.record_imported_name_edit(&mut changes, alias, new_imported_name);
+                }
+                EditDecision::No => continue,
+                EditDecision::Omit => return None,
+            }
+        }

+        (!changes.is_empty()).then_some(changes)
+    }

+    /// Computes imported name and module name edits for an import-from statement.
+    ///
+    /// For example, `from pkg import old` becomes `from pkg import new`, and
+    /// `from pkg.old import C` becomes `from pkg.new import C`.
+    ///
+    /// Returns `None` when the module cannot be resolved or the rename produces no source edits
+    /// or bound name changes.

+        statement: &ast::StmtImportFrom,
+        module_member_name_analyzer: &mut ModuleMemberNameAnalyzer<'_, 'db>,

+            statement.level,

+            .module_name_changes
+            .new_module_name(resolved_module.name(self.model.db()))

+            let module = statement.module.as_ref()?;
+            Some(self.import_from_module_edit(module, new_module_name))
+        } else {
+            None
+        };
+
+        let mut changes = ImportStatementChanges::default();
+        for alias in &statement.names {
+            match self.should_edit_imported_name_for_import_from(
+                alias,
+                resolved_module,
+                module_member_name_analyzer,
+            ) {
+                EditDecision::Yes(new_imported_name) => {
+                    self.record_imported_name_edit(&mut changes, alias, new_imported_name);
+                }
+                EditDecision::No | EditDecision::Omit => continue,
+            }
+        }

+        // An import-from statement may still have a module name edit when no imported names change.
+        if let Some(import_from_module_edit) = import_from_module_edit {
+            changes.edits.push(import_from_module_edit);
+        }
+
+        (!changes.is_empty()).then_some(changes)
+    }

+    /// in the statement `import pkg.old`).

+//! Computes source edits for Python file renames.
+//!
+//! ## Overview
+//!
+//! [`will_rename_files`] maps filesystem renames to module names, then computes edits for import
+//! statements and references in indexed project files. It does not move files, discover package
+//! contents, validate the filesystem operation, or normalize the returned edits.
+//!
+//! EXAMPLE:
+//!
+//! When `pkg/old.py` is renamed to `pkg/new.py`, the following code:
+//!
+//! ```python
+//! from pkg import old
+//! print(old.C)
+//! ```
+//!
+//! is updated like so:
+//!
+//! ```python
+//! from pkg import new
+//! print(new.C)
+//! ```
+//!
+//! [`will_rename_files`] computes edits over all files in parallel using [`edits_for_file`]. That
+//! in turn computes edits for a single file in two distinct AST passes: [`ImportStatementVisitor`]
+//! visits import statements and computes edits for them, then [`ModuleReferenceVisitor`] visits
+//! all references to imported modules and computes edits for those references. Those two sets of
+//! edits are combined to produce the final result.
+//!
+//! ## Terminology
+//!
+//! Below is the anatomy of the two types of import statement.
+//!
+//! A "plain" import statement:
+//!
+//! ```text
+//!              Alias
+//!        +---------------+
+//! import pkg.old as stable
+//!        |          |
+//!        |          explicit alias
+//!        imported name
+//! ```
+//!
+//! and an "import-from" statement:
+//!
+//! ```text
+//!                       Alias
+//!                   +-----------+
+//! from ..pkg import old as stable
+//!      | |            |      |
+//!      | module name  |      explicit alias
+//!      |              imported name
+//!      |
+//!      import level
+//! ```
+//!
+//! From there, we can layer on a few additional terms.
+//!
+//! | Term | Meaning | Example |
+//! | --- | --- | --- |
+//! | Bound name | A name introduced by an import. | `stable` in both diagrams. |
+//! | Module reference | The use of a module in an expression. | `old` in `old.C`; `pkg.old` in `pkg.old.C`. |
+//! | Re-export | A name that a module imports from elsewhere and makes available through its own namespace. | `facade.py`: `from pkg import old`; elsewhere: `from facade import old`. |
+//! | Imported name edit | Replacement of an imported name. | `import old` → `import new`, `import pkg.old` → `import pkg.new` |
+//! | Module name edit | Replacement of the module name in an import-from statement. | `from old import C` → `from new import C`. |
+//! | Bound name change | Change to a bound name caused by an imported name edit. | `old` → `new`; no bound name change for an explicit alias like `as stable`. |
+//! | Reference edit | Replacement at a module reference. | `old.C` → `new.C`. |
+//! | Source edit | Source range and replacement text. | Range of `old`, replacement `new`. |
+//!
+//! The above terms are used consistently throughout this module.

+/// Computes source edits for a batch of Python file renames.
+///
+/// The following types of rename request are not yet supported:
+///
+/// - A request that renames a directory
+/// - A request that changes a module parent (e.g., renaming `a.old` to `b.new` or `new`)
+/// - A request that renames an `__init__.py` or `__init__.pyi` file
+/// - A request that changes the extension of a module (e.g., from `.py` to `.pyi`)
+///
+/// When a rename batch contains both supported and unsupported requests, the unsupported requests
+/// are skipped while the supported ones produce edits as normal.
+///
+/// The returned edits refer to the original files and source ranges. The caller must sort the edits
+/// and handle duplicates and overlaps before applying them.
+///
+/// ## Unsupported edits
+///
+/// Even for supported renames, some occurrences are not updated:
+///
+/// - Name references supplied by star imports, such as `from pkg import *`.
+/// - Names in `global` and `nonlocal` declarations, and references whose resolution crosses those
+///   declarations.
+/// - Names and attributes being assigned to or deleted. Receiver expressions can still be updated.
+/// - Names in ordinary strings, including `__all__` entries and dynamic imports (although module
+///   references in string annotations are supported).
+///
+/// Other edits may still be returned, so an import can be updated while a reference to its old
+/// name remains unchanged.
+///
+/// Additionally, an ambiguous imported name is left unchanged even when other names in the same
+/// import-from statement are updated. For example, suppose we rename `old.py` to `new.py` and
+/// `other.py` to `another.py`:
+///
+/// ```python
+/// # facade.py
+/// import old
+/// import other
+/// if flag:
+///     old = 0
+///
+/// # use.py
+/// from facade import other, old
+/// ```
+///
+/// In the import from `facade`, `old` may or may not refer to the renamed module, so it is left
+/// unchanged. The import becomes `from facade import another, old`.
+fn will_rename_files(db: &dyn Db, renames: &[FileRename]) -> Vec<FileRenameEdit> {
+    let files: Vec<_> = db.project().files(db).iter().collect();
+    let module_name_changes = ModuleNameChanges::new(db, renames);
+    if module_name_changes.is_empty() {
+        return Vec::new();
+    }
+
+    files
+        .into_par_iter()
+        .map_with_db(db, |db, file| {
+            edits_for_file(db, file, &module_name_changes)
+        })
+        .flatten()
+        .collect()
+}

+/// One Python file rename in a batch.
+struct FileRename {
+    /// The source file before the rename.
+    file: File,
+    /// The destination path, which need not exist yet.
+    new_path: SystemPathBuf,
+}
+
+/// A replacement and the file range containing it.
+type FileRenameEdit = RangedValue<String>;
+
+/// Maps old module names to new module names for supported file renames.
+struct ModuleNameChanges<'db> {
+    // A map from old module name to new module name for supported rename operations.
+    module_renames: FxHashMap<&'db ModuleName, ModuleName>,
+    // The module basename for each key in `module_renames` (e.g., `old` in `pkg.old`).
+    old_module_basenames: FxHashSet<&'db str>,
+    // Used to check whether a source file may contain an old module basename.
+    old_module_basename_matchers: Vec<NameMatcher<'db>>,
+}
+
+impl<'db> ModuleNameChanges<'db> {
+    fn new(db: &'db dyn Db, renames: &[FileRename]) -> Self {
+        let module_renames: FxHashMap<_, _> = renames
+            .iter()
+            .filter_map(|rename| module_rename(db, rename))
+            .filter(|(old_module_name, new_module_name)| *old_module_name != new_module_name)
+            .collect();
+        let old_module_basenames: FxHashSet<&'db str> = module_renames
+            .keys()
+            .map(|&module_name| module_name.last_component())
+            .collect();
+        let old_module_basename_matchers = old_module_basenames
+            .iter()
+            .map(|&basename| NameMatcher::new(basename))
+            .collect();
+        Self {
+            module_renames,
+            old_module_basenames,
+            old_module_basename_matchers,
+        }
+    }
+
+    fn is_empty(&self) -> bool {
+        self.module_renames.is_empty()
+    }
+
+    fn new_module_name(&self, old_module_name: &ModuleName) -> Option<&ModuleName> {
+        self.module_renames.get(old_module_name)
+    }
+
+    fn is_old_module_basename(&self, name: &str) -> bool {
+        self.old_module_basenames.contains(name)
+    }
+
+    /// Returns whether the source may need edits for these module name changes.
+    fn may_affect_source(&self, source: &str) -> bool {
+        self.old_module_basename_matchers
+            .iter()
+            .any(|matcher| matcher.may_match(source))
+    }
+}

+/// Computes edits for one candidate file in two AST passes.
+///
+/// 1. [`ImportStatementVisitor`] traverses import statements in the AST to compute edits to those
+///    statements specifically, and to record bound name changes.
+/// 2. [`ModuleReferenceVisitor`] traverses many different AST nodes to computes edits to each
+///    reference to an imported module. Reaching definitions determine which module references need
+///    updating after a bound name change.
+///
+/// Computing import statement edits first lets us base reference edits on the bound name changes,
+/// accounting for explicit aliases and re-exports. A rejected imported name edit leaves its
+/// bound name unchanged.
+fn edits_for_file(
+    db: &dyn Db,
+    file: File,
+    module_name_changes: &ModuleNameChanges<'_>,
+) -> Vec<FileRenameEdit> {
+    let program_file = db.program_file(file);
+    let source = source_text(db, file);
+    if !module_name_changes.may_affect_source(&source) {
+        return Vec::new();
+    }
+
+    let parsed_module = ruff_db::parsed::parsed_module(db, program_file.python_file(db)).load(db);
+    let root = AnyNodeRef::from(parsed_module.syntax());
+    let model = SemanticModel::new(db, program_file);
+    let mut bound_name_change_cache = BoundNameChangeCache::new(module_name_changes);
+
+    let import_statement_changes = {
+        let mut import_statement_visitor =
+            ImportStatementVisitor::new(db, &model, &mut bound_name_change_cache);
+        root.visit_source_order(&mut import_statement_visitor);
+        import_statement_visitor.changes
+    };
+
+    let mut module_reference_visitor = ModuleReferenceVisitor::new(
+        db,
+        &model,
+        &source,
+        &import_statement_changes.bound_name_changes,
+        &mut bound_name_change_cache,
+    );
+    root.visit_source_order(&mut module_reference_visitor);
+
+    let mut edits = import_statement_changes.edits;
+    edits.extend(module_reference_visitor.edits);
+    edits
+}

+/// Computes imported name and module name edits, and records bound name changes.

+    // Plain import statements and import-from statements cannot occur inside expressions.

+}
+
+impl<'a, 'db> ImportStatementEditor<'a, 'db> {

+        Self {

+    ///

+    fn edit_plain_import(

+            match self.should_edit_imported_name_for_plain_import(alias) {

+    /// Computes imported name and module name edits for an import-from statement.

+    ///

+    fn edit_import_from(

+                resolved_module,
+                module_member_name_analyzer,

+                EditDecision::Yes(new_imported_name) => {

+        (!changes.is_empty()).then_some(changes)

+    /// Chooses an imported name edit for a plain import statement (e.g., `pkg.old` to `pkg.new`
+    /// in the statement `import pkg.old`).
+    fn should_edit_imported_name_for_plain_import(&self, alias: &ast::Alias) -> EditDecision {
+        let Some(resolved_module) = self.model.resolve_module(Some(alias.name.as_str()), 0) else {
+            return EditDecision::No;
+        };
+
+        let Some(new_module_name) = self
+            .module_name_changes
+            .new_module_name(resolved_module.name(self.model.db()))

+            return EditDecision::No;
+        };

+    ///
+    /// For example, renaming `pkg.old` can change the imported name `old` in both
+    /// `from pkg import old` and `from facade import old` when `facade` re-exports `old`.
+    fn should_edit_imported_name_for_import_from(
+        &self,
+        alias: &ast::Alias,
+        resolved_module: Module<'db>,
+        module_member_name_analyzer: &mut ModuleMemberNameAnalyzer<'_, 'db>,
+    ) -> EditDecision {

+            .module_name_changes
+            .is_old_module_basename(alias.name.as_str())
+        {
+            return EditDecision::No;
+        }
+
+        if let Some(imported_module) = self.directly_imported_submodule(alias, resolved_module) {
+            let Some(new_module_name) = self
+                .module_name_changes
+                .new_module_name(imported_module.name(self.model.db()))
+            else {
+                return EditDecision::No;
+            };
+
+            return EditDecision::replace_if_changed(
+                alias.name.as_str(),
+                new_module_name.last_component(),
+            );
+        }

+    /// Constructs a module name edit, preserving its prefix and the import level.
+    ///
+    /// The module parent is unchanged, so only the final component needs replacing.
+    /// For example, `from ..pkg.old import C` becomes `from ..pkg.new import C`.
+    fn import_from_module_edit(
+        &self,
+        module: &ast::Identifier,
+        new_module_name: &ModuleName,
+    ) -> FileRenameEdit {
+        let replacement = if let Some((prefix, _)) = module.as_str().rsplit_once('.') {
+            format!("{prefix}.{}", new_module_name.last_component())
+        } else {
+            new_module_name.last_component().to_string()
+        };
+        self.source_edit(module.range, replacement)
+    }
+
+    /// Identifies an imported name that resolves to a direct submodule.
+    ///
+    /// For example, `old` in `from pkg import old` when it resolves to `pkg/old.py`.
+    fn directly_imported_submodule(
+        &self,
+        alias: &ast::Alias,
+        resolved_module: Module<'db>,
+    ) -> Option<Module<'db>> {
+        let db = self.model.db();
+        let module_name = resolved_module.name(db);
+        let imported_module = resolved_module_from_type(self.model, alias)?;
+        let imported_module_name = imported_module.name(db);
+
+        if alias.name.as_str() != imported_module_name.last_component()
+            || imported_module_name.parent().as_ref() != Some(module_name)
+        {
+            return None;
+        }
+
+        // Without a package definition for `old`, `from pkg import old` imports `pkg.old`
+        // directly (for example, when `pkg/__init__.py` is empty).
+        if self
+            .model
+            .definitions_for_module_global(resolved_module, alias.name.as_str())
+            .is_none()
+        {
+            return Some(imported_module);
+        }
+
+        // In `pkg/__init__.py`, `from . import old` imports `pkg.old` directly and defines
+        // the package's `old` bound name. Resolving that name as a re-export would analyze
+        // the same import again.
+        if file_to_module(db, self.model.program_file().resolver_file(db))
+            .is_some_and(|importing_module| importing_module.name(db) == module_name)
+        {
+            return Some(imported_module);
+        }
+
+        None
+    }
+
+    /// Records an imported name edit and any resulting bound name change.
+    ///
+    /// For example, renaming `pkg/old.py` to `pkg/new.py` changes the imported name `pkg.old` in
+    /// `import pkg.old` to `pkg.new`, but keeps the bound name `pkg`. Conversely, the same rename
+    /// changes the imported name `old` in `from pkg import old` to `new` and also changes the bound
+    /// name.
+    fn record_imported_name_edit(
+        &self,
+        changes: &mut ImportStatementChanges<'db>,
+        alias: &ast::Alias,
+        new_imported_name: String,
+    ) {
+        if let Some(new_bound_name) = Self::bound_name_replacement(alias, &new_imported_name) {
+            let definition =
+                ty_python_core::semantic_index(self.model.db(), self.model.program_file())
+                    .expect_single_definition(alias);
+            changes
+                .bound_name_changes
+                .insert(definition, new_bound_name.to_owned());
+        }
+
+        changes
+            .edits
+            .push(self.source_edit(alias.name.range, new_imported_name));
+    }
+
+    /// Constructs a source edit, such as replacing the imported name `old` with `new`.
+    fn source_edit(&self, range: TextRange, replacement: String) -> FileRenameEdit {
+        RangedValue {
+            range: FileRange::new(self.model.file(), range),
+            value: replacement,
+        }
+    }
+
+    /// Returns the new bound name if changing the imported name also changes its binding.
+    fn bound_name_replacement<'name>(
+        alias: &ast::Alias,
+        new_imported_name: &'name str,
+    ) -> Option<&'name str> {
+        if alias.asname.is_some() {
+            return None;
+        }
+
+        // `import pkg.old` binds `pkg`, while `from pkg import old` binds `old`.
+        // The first component of the imported name gives the bound name in both cases.
+        let old_bound_name = Self::first_component(alias.name.as_str());
+        let new_bound_name = Self::first_component(new_imported_name);
+        (old_bound_name != new_bound_name).then_some(new_bound_name)
+    }
+
+    /// Retrieves the first component of an imported name: `pkg` for `pkg.old`, or `old` for `old`.
+    fn first_component(alias_name: &str) -> &str {
+        alias_name
+            .split_once('.')
+            .map(|(first, _)| first)
+            .unwrap_or(alias_name)
+    }
+}
+
+type BoundNameChanges<'db> = FxHashMap<Definition<'db>, String>;
+
+#[derive(Default)]
+struct ImportStatementChanges<'db> {
+    /// Source edits to imported names and module names.
+    edits: Vec<FileRenameEdit>,
+    /// Maps import definitions to new bound names for reference edits.
+    bound_name_changes: BoundNameChanges<'db>,
+}
+
+impl ImportStatementChanges<'_> {
+    fn is_empty(&self) -> bool {
+        self.edits.is_empty() && self.bound_name_changes.is_empty()
+    }
+
+    fn extend(&mut self, other: Self) {
+        self.edits.extend(other.edits);
+        self.bound_name_changes.extend(other.bound_name_changes);
+    }
+}
+
+/// Caches bound name decisions by import definition while computing edits for one file.
+struct BoundNameChangeCache<'db> {
+    module_name_changes: &'db ModuleNameChanges<'db>,
+    bound_name_decisions_by_import: FxHashMap<Definition<'db>, EditDecision>,
+}
+
+impl<'db> BoundNameChangeCache<'db> {
+    fn new(module_name_changes: &'db ModuleNameChanges<'db>) -> Self {
+        Self {
+            module_name_changes,
+            bound_name_decisions_by_import: FxHashMap::default(),
+        }
+    }
+}
+
+/// Computes an edit decision for a module member name after a file rename.
+struct ModuleMemberNameAnalyzer<'cache, 'db> {
+    db: &'db dyn Db,
+    cache: &'cache mut BoundNameChangeCache<'db>,
+    import_definitions_in_progress: FxHashSet<Definition<'db>>,
+    import_cycle_detected: bool,
+}
+
+impl<'cache, 'db> ModuleMemberNameAnalyzer<'cache, 'db> {
+    fn new(db: &'db dyn Db, cache: &'cache mut BoundNameChangeCache<'db>) -> Self {
+        Self {
+            db,
+            cache,
+            import_definitions_in_progress: FxHashSet::default(),
+            import_cycle_detected: false,
+        }
+    }
+
+    /// Decides whether to edit `bound_name` when it is imported from `resolved_module`
+    /// (e.g., `old` in `from facade import old`) or accessed as an attribute
+    /// (e.g., `old` in `facade.old`).
+    ///
+    /// This follows import definitions through re-exports. An explicit alias preserves the bound
+    /// name even when the imported name changes.
+    ///
+    /// A `Yes` decision requires every possible definition to produce the same replacement; `No`
+    /// requires every definition to preserve the name. Otherwise, the method returns `Omit`.
+    /// For example:
+    ///
+    /// ```python
+    /// # facade.py
+    /// if flag:
+    ///     from pkg import old
+    /// else:
+    ///     old = 1
+    /// ```
+    ///
+    /// Renaming `pkg.old` to `pkg.new` changes the imported name to `new`, but the assignment
+    /// keeps `old`. Neither name works in both branches, so the method returns `Omit` for `old`.
+    ///
+    /// Missing definitions and disagreements between a stub and its runtime module also lead to
+    /// `Omit`. If a cycle is detected, this method returns `Omit` without caching the affected
+    /// bound name changes.
+    fn should_edit_module_member(
+        &mut self,
+        model: &SemanticModel<'db>,
+        resolved_module: Module<'db>,
+        bound_name: &str,
+    ) -> EditDecision {
+        // A cycle in one name must not affect the next name in the same import statement.
+        if self.import_definitions_in_progress.is_empty() {
+            self.import_cycle_detected = false;
+        }
+
+        let db = self.db;
+        let decision = self.should_edit_member_in_module(model, resolved_module, bound_name);
+        if decision == EditDecision::Omit {
+            return decision;
+        }
+
+        // A stub can expose a different bound name;
+        // propagate only those changes that both facets agree on.
+        if let Some(runtime_module) =
+            resolve_real_module_confident(db, resolver_environment(db), resolved_module.name(db))
+            && runtime_module.file(db) != resolved_module.file(db)
+            && self.should_edit_member_in_module(model, runtime_module, bound_name) != decision
+        {
+            return EditDecision::Omit;
+        }
+
+        decision
+    }
+
+    fn should_edit_member_in_module(
+        &mut self,
+        model: &SemanticModel<'db>,
+        module: Module<'db>,
+        bound_name: &str,
+    ) -> EditDecision {
+        let Some(resolution) = model.definitions_for_module_global(module, bound_name) else {
+            return EditDecision::Omit;
+        };
+        let mut builder = EditDecisionBuilder::new(&resolution);
+
+        for &definition in resolution.definitions() {
+            if builder.edit_is_omitted() {
+                break;
+            }
+            builder.add(self.should_edit_arbitrary_definition(definition));
+        }
+
+        builder.finish()
+    }
+
+    fn should_edit_arbitrary_definition(&mut self, definition: Definition<'db>) -> EditDecision {
+        let db = self.db;
+        // An import in a non-indexed file keeps its bound name.
+        if !db.project().files(db).contains(definition.file(db)) {
+            return EditDecision::No;
+        }
+
+        let parsed_module = ruff_db::parsed::parsed_module(db, definition.python_file(db)).load(db);
+        let model = SemanticModel::new(db, definition.program_file(db));
+        let module_name_changes = self.cache.module_name_changes;
+
+        match definition.kind(db) {
+            DefinitionKind::Import(import) => {
+                let alias = import.alias(&parsed_module);
+                self.should_edit_import_definition(definition, alias, |_| {
+                    ImportStatementEditor::new(&model, module_name_changes)
+                        .should_edit_imported_name_for_plain_import(alias)
+                })
+            }
+            DefinitionKind::ImportFrom(import) => {
+                let statement = import.import(&parsed_module);
+                let alias = import.alias(&parsed_module);
+                self.should_edit_import_definition(
+                    definition,
+                    alias,
+                    |module_member_name_analyzer| {
+                        let Some(resolved_module) = model.resolve_module(
+                            statement.module.as_ref().map(ast::Identifier::as_str),
+                            statement.level,
+                        ) else {
+                            return EditDecision::Omit;
+                        };
+
+                        ImportStatementEditor::new(&model, module_name_changes)
+                            .should_edit_imported_name_for_import_from(
+                                alias,
+                                resolved_module,
+                                module_member_name_analyzer,
+                            )
+                    },
+                )
+            }
+            DefinitionKind::StarImport(_) | DefinitionKind::ImportFromSubmodule(_) => {
+                EditDecision::Omit
+            }
+            _ => EditDecision::No,
+        }
+    }
+
+    /// Determines and caches whether the bound name introduced by an import definition changes.
+    ///
+    /// Revisiting a definition while its analysis is in progress detects a cycle. Cyclic results
+    /// are not cached because their outcome can depend on where the analysis started.
+    fn should_edit_import_definition(
+        &mut self,
+        import_definition: Definition<'db>,
+        alias: &ast::Alias,
+        should_edit_imported_name: impl FnOnce(&mut Self) -> EditDecision,
+    ) -> EditDecision {
+        if self.import_cycle_detected {
+            return EditDecision::Omit;
+        }
+
+        if let Some(decision) = self
+            .cache
+            .bound_name_decisions_by_import
+            .get(&import_definition)
+        {
+            return decision.clone();
+        }
+
+        if !self
+            .import_definitions_in_progress
+            .insert(import_definition)
+        {
+            self.import_cycle_detected = true;
+            return EditDecision::Omit;
+        }
+
+        let imported_name_decision = should_edit_imported_name(self);
+        self.import_definitions_in_progress
+            .remove(&import_definition);
+        if self.import_cycle_detected {
+            return EditDecision::Omit;
+        }
+
+        let decision = match imported_name_decision {
+            EditDecision::Yes(new_imported_name) => {
+                ImportStatementEditor::bound_name_replacement(alias, &new_imported_name)
+                    .map(|name| EditDecision::Yes(name.to_owned()))
+                    .unwrap_or(EditDecision::No)
+            }
+            // An omitted imported name edit leaves the binding unchanged.
+            EditDecision::No | EditDecision::Omit => EditDecision::No,
+        };
+        self.cache
+            .bound_name_decisions_by_import
+            .insert(import_definition, decision.clone());
+        decision
+    }
+}
+
+/// Computes reference edits for renamed modules.
+///
+/// For example, when `from pkg import old` becomes `from pkg import new`,
+/// this visitor computes an edit to change a module reference such as
+///
+/// ```python
+/// old.C
+/// ```
+///
+/// to
+///
+/// ```python
+/// new.C
+/// ```
+///
+/// It also rewrites module references through attributes: renaming `pkg.old`
+/// to `pkg.new` can change `pkg.old.C` to `pkg.new.C`.
+///
+/// For module references through names, reaching definitions connect each
+/// reference to the bound name changes recorded by [`ImportStatementVisitor`].
+/// For module references through attributes, the visitor uses module types and, when the receiver
+/// defines the attribute, [`ModuleMemberNameAnalyzer`] to decide whether and how to edit it.
+struct ModuleReferenceVisitor<'a, 'db> {
+    db: &'db dyn Db,
+    model: &'a SemanticModel<'db>,
+    source: &'a str,
+    module_name_changes: &'a ModuleNameChanges<'db>,
+    bound_name_changes: &'a BoundNameChanges<'db>,
+    bound_name_change_cache: &'a mut BoundNameChangeCache<'db>,
+    in_string_annotation: bool,
+    edits: Vec<FileRenameEdit>,
+}
+
+impl<'a, 'db> ModuleReferenceVisitor<'a, 'db> {
+    fn new(
+        db: &'db dyn Db,
+        model: &'a SemanticModel<'db>,
+        source: &'a str,
+        bound_name_changes: &'a BoundNameChanges<'db>,
+        bound_name_change_cache: &'a mut BoundNameChangeCache<'db>,
+    ) -> Self {
+        Self {
+            db,
+            model,
+            source,
+            module_name_changes: bound_name_change_cache.module_name_changes,
+            bound_name_changes,
+            bound_name_change_cache,
+            in_string_annotation: false,
+            edits: Vec::new(),
+        }
+    }
+
+    /// Chooses a reference edit for a name by considering the definitions that connect that name
+    /// to a bound name change from an import statement.
+    fn edit_name_reference(&mut self, name: &ast::ExprName) {
+        let Some(resolution) = self.model.reaching_definitions(name) else {
+            return;
+        };
+
+        if resolution.crosses_scope_declaration() {
+            // Renaming a name declared `global` or `nonlocal` also requires updating its
+            // declaration and writes; this is not yet supported.
+            return;
+        }
+
+        let mut builder = EditDecisionBuilder::new(&resolution);
+
+        for &definition in resolution.definitions() {
+            if builder.edit_is_omitted() {
+                break;
+            }
+            let decision = if matches!(definition.kind(self.db), DefinitionKind::StarImport(_)) {
+                // Module references introduced by star imports such as `from pkg import *`
+                // are unsupported.
+                EditDecision::Omit
+            } else if let Some(replacement) = self.bound_name_changes.get(&definition) {
+                EditDecision::Yes(replacement.clone())
+            } else {
+                EditDecision::No
+            };
+            builder.add(decision);
+        }
+
+        self.record_reference_edit(name.range(), builder.finish());
+    }
+
+    /// Chooses a reference edit for an attribute such as `pkg.old`.
+    ///
+    /// Both the attribute and its receiver must resolve to modules.
+    /// For attributes defined in the receiver's module, [`ModuleMemberNameAnalyzer`] determines
+    /// whether their names change.
+    fn edit_attribute_reference(&mut self, attribute: &ast::ExprAttribute) {
+        if !attribute.ctx.is_load() {
+            // Do not rewrite an attribute name that is assigned to or deleted.
+            // The visitor still traverses the receiver, so renaming `pkg.old` to `pkg.new`
+            // can change `pkg.old.VALUE = 1` to `pkg.new.VALUE = 1`.
+            return;
+        }
+
+        let Some(attribute_module) = resolved_module_from_type(self.model, attribute) else {
+            return;
+        };
+        let old_module_name = attribute_module.name(self.db);
+        let Some(new_module_name) = self.module_name_changes.new_module_name(old_module_name)
+        else {
+            return;
+        };
+        let Some(receiver_module) = resolved_module_from_type(self.model, &*attribute.value) else {
+            return;
+        };
+
+        let attribute_name = attribute.attr.as_str();
+
+        // Computes a necessary condition for rewriting a direct submodule reference.
+        //
+        // Consider this example (when we're renaming `pkg/old.py` to `pkg/new.py`):
+        //
+        // ```python
+        // holder.old = pkg.old # A
+        // print(holder.old)    # B
+        // ```
+        //
+        // For A, we want to rewrite `pkg.old` to `pkg.new`. There, `pkg.old`
+        // (the old module name) relative to `pkg` (the receiver) is `old`
+        // (the attribute name), so the attribute does indeed match the
+        // old module name and we should rewrite it.
+        //
+        // For B, we do not want to rewrite `holder.old` to `holder.new`, even though
+        // `holder.old` refers to the `pkg.old` module. There, `pkg.old` relative to
+        // `holder` is `None`, so the attribute does
+        // not match the old module name and we do not rewrite it.
+        let attribute_matches_old_module_name = old_module_name
+            .relative_to(receiver_module.name(self.db))
+            .is_some_and(|relative_name| relative_name.as_str() == attribute_name);

body: Could we check that the first lookup actually runs `place_by_id` before we clear the events? Since we refer to the query by name, a rename would silently make this assertion pass even if the renamed query ran on every edit.

Could we also assert which variant we get for each maximum? These values would all round-trip if `PackedIds` always chose `Full`. The previous test checked the storage width too, and it would be good to keep that coverage at the `U8` and `U16` boundaries.

Could we use the same check for unspecialized type variables here and in the general walker? Consider `type Phantom[X] = int` and an evidence bound `T ≤ list[Phantom[UnspecializedTypeVar]]`. This fast path expands `Phantom` to `int`, so it misses the marker and retains the bound. Under `Ignore`, the general walker inspects the alias arguments and drops the same bound.

I’d expect the solution for `T` to stay the same when we add an unrelated `(U = int) or (U = str)` constraint. That would be a way to exercise both paths in a solver test.

+## Recursive calls preserve captured type variables
+
+A recursive call can infer a new specialization of the function's type parameter. A nested function
+that captures that parameter still refers to the original argument's type. Comparing a generic
+callback with that captured type also leaves the original parameter unchanged.
+
+```py
+from collections.abc import Callable
+
+def recursive[T](value: T) -> T:
+    def captured(other: T) -> T:
+        return other
+
+    def generic[U](other: U) -> U:
+        return other
+
+    def accepts(callback: Callable[[T], T]) -> None: ...
+
+    accepts(generic)  # no diagnostic
+    captured(1)  # error: [invalid-argument-type]
+    # revealed: Literal[1]
+    reveal_type(recursive(1))
+    # revealed: T@recursive
+    reveal_type(captured(value))
+    return recursive(value)  # no diagnostic
+```
+
+## Type parameter defaults referring to other parameters
+
+Defaults use the type arguments inferred for the same call, including when the argument's type is
+fixed by an enclosing generic function.
+
+```toml
+[environment]
+python-version = "3.13"
+```
+
+```py
+def defaults[T, U = list[T], V = tuple[U, T]](value: T) -> tuple[U, V]:
+    raise NotImplementedError
+
+def check[T](value: T) -> tuple[list[T], tuple[list[T], T]]:
+    result = defaults(value)

+## Capturing an enclosing type parameter
+
+An alias defined inside a generic function refers to that function's type parameter.
+
+```py
+def outer[T](value: T) -> T:
+    type Captured = T
+
+    def identity(other: Captured) -> Captured:
+        return other
+
+    return identity(value)  # no diagnostic
+```
+
+The alias can also have its own parameters. Specializing them preserves the captured parameter.

+
+```toml
+target-version = "py311"
+
+[lint]
+preview = true
+select = ["ASYNC401"]

+## Exception groups
+
+Without additional checks, `pytest.raises` checks the group's type without
+checking its contents. Use `pytest.RaisesGroup` to specify the expected
+exceptions.
+
+```py
+import pytest
+
+with pytest.raises(ExceptionGroup):  # snapshot: pytest-raises-exception-group
+    raise ExceptionGroup("errors", [ValueError()])
+```
+
+```snapshot
+error[ASYNC401]: Prefer `pytest.RaisesGroup` over an exception group type
+ --> src/mdtest_snippet.py:3:20
+  |
+3 | with pytest.raises(ExceptionGroup):  # snapshot: pytest-raises-exception-group
+  |                    ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
+help: Use `pytest.RaisesGroup` to specify the expected exceptions
+```
+
+```py
+with pytest.raises(BaseExceptionGroup):  # error: [pytest-raises-exception-group]
+    raise BaseExceptionGroup("errors", [KeyboardInterrupt()])
+
+with pytest.RaisesGroup(ValueError):
+    raise ExceptionGroup("errors", [ValueError()])
+
+with pytest.RaisesGroup(KeyboardInterrupt):
+    raise BaseExceptionGroup("errors", [KeyboardInterrupt()])
+
+with pytest.raises(ValueError):
+    raise ValueError()
+```
+
+## Expected exception arguments
+
+The expected exception can be passed by position or keyword, or included in a
+tuple. A call produces one diagnostic even if it contains multiple group types.
+
+```py
+import pytest
+
+pytest.raises(ExceptionGroup)  # error: [pytest-raises-exception-group]
+pytest.raises(expected_exception=BaseExceptionGroup)  # error: [pytest-raises-exception-group]
+pytest.raises((ValueError, ExceptionGroup))  # error: [pytest-raises-exception-group]
+pytest.raises((ExceptionGroup, BaseExceptionGroup))  # error: [pytest-raises-exception-group]
+pytest.raises((ValueError, (TypeError, BaseExceptionGroup)))  # error: [pytest-raises-exception-group]

Main accepts this call, but the PR rejects `takes_int` because it expects a callback that accepts `object`.

```python
from collections.abc import Callable, Sequence

def f[T, U, **P](cb: Callable[[T], None], x: U) -> tuple[list[T], list[U]]:
    raise NotImplementedError

def takes_int(x: int) -> None:
    pass

result: tuple[list[object] | list[int], list[str] | Sequence[int]] = f(takes_int, 0)
```

Main already rejects `takes_int` if I add a third parameter `seed: T` to `f` and pass a value of type `int`. In that case `T` has both a lower and an upper bound of `int`. On the legacy retry, the lower bound is compatible with the preferred `object`, but the callback’s upper bound rules it out. This PR extends the rejection to the call above, where the callback supplies the only bound. `T = U = int` works for both slots of the result. Could we check the preferred type against the callback’s upper bound on retry?

I reran the `TypedDict.get` large-literal-union benchmark input with the base and PR CLI binaries. The median of three runs went from 0.349 s to 0.455 s at 1,024 literals and from 0.425 s to 0.790 s at 2,048. At 1,024 literals, CodSpeed’s simulated CPU time also went from 369 ms to 1,524 ms (4.1×) on this head. [CodSpeed report](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/26680#issuecomment-4929590099)

These two disjointness filters compare members against the opposite union. Could we skip literals shared by both unions before doing those checks? This is the pattern covered by [astral-sh/ty#4419](https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/4419).

I suspect this could be a significant part of e.g. the pydantic regression?

This rejects a valid callback even when the call has no expected return type.

```python
from collections.abc import Callable
from typing import TypedDict

def keys_for[T](get: Callable[[T], int]) -> list[T]:
    return []

class Payload(TypedDict):
    count: int

def example(data: Payload) -> None:
    keys_for(data.__getitem__)
```

The base infers `list[Literal["count"]]`. The PR promotes `T` to `str`, but the arbitrary-key overload returns `object`, so the callback fails the argument check. Could we preserve the literal when promotion would violate an argument-derived upper bound? The same example reproduces on the legacy path with an unused `**P`.

The slowdown in your example isn't caused by the alias traversal here, it's the fixpoint iteration itself. The same blowup can be seen on main with 16 inline `T | dict[str, T]` parameters, so it doesn't seem like this is a problem in practice? We could add a maximum cap on the number of fixpoint iterations if it does because a problem.

There are a number of existing issues around "pollution" during fixpoint inference (see https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/3934), especially around `TypedDict`. In your example, we should be able to infer `Row` without the outer `copy` call (we currently infer `Row | dict[str, int]`), the outer fixpoint iteration is just masking the issue. Changing `first` to return `list[T]` also exposes the failure. Part of the goal of this PR was to avoid cases where `reveal_type` and similar were hiding existing limitations in our generic inference, so I think a regression in that specific example is fine.

So for this example:

```python
from copy import copy
from typing import TypedDict

class Row(TypedDict):
    id: int

def first[T](values: list[T]) -> T:
    return values[0]

def example(row: Row):
    result = copy(first([row, {"id": 1}]))
    checked: Row = result
```

On main we infer `Row` for `result = ...`, but on this PR we infer `Row | dict[str, int]` and error on the last line. I think it's because we're skipping the second pass for `copy`? Should we _not_ skip iteration when the argument itself is a generic call?

It seems like this _can_ get very expensive:

```python
type Value[T] = T | dict[str, T]

def collect[T](*values: Value[T]) -> None: pass

collect(
    {"x": 1}, {"x": 1}, {"x": 1}, {"x": 1},
    {"x": 1}, {"x": 1}, {"x": 1}, {"x": 1},
    {"x": 1}, {"x": 1}, {"x": 1}, {"x": 1},
    {"x": 1}, {"x": 1}, {"x": 1}, {"x": 1},
)
```

This is 34ms on main and >2 seconds on the PR (at least with a debug build). Any good ideas?

Passing the full method signature here exposes the (pre-existing, and already reproducible via ParamSpac) assumption made in lambda inference that the expected parameters are positional. For example, this is a valid replacement, swapping the order of keyword-only parameters:

```py

> A merged baseline can contain both spellings. I verified that Git can cleanly merge an `unresolved-import` entry from one branch with an `import-not-found` entry for the same file from another. A narrow fix is to use the old spelling for sorting only when the file uses it consistently, and retain current-name ordering when both spellings occur.

There's an extension of this that we should fix in this PR:

```py
def size[Tag](tag: Tag, values: list[int]) -> int:
    return len(values)

def _(rows: list[int | None]):
    # currently: list[Unknown]
    # should be: list[int]
    index_of(rows, size(0, reveal_type([])))
```

per codex:

> On the second pass, `size` receives `int | None` as inferred context. Both the `int` and `None` attempts succeed because the new check compares the return type `int` against the entire union. Two successes trigger the fallback that infers the arguments without context. That makes the empty list reveal `list[Unknown]`, even though `size` always requires `list[int]`. Rejecting targets disjoint from the return type would eliminate the `None` attempt while still allowing a union-valued result to overlap several targets.

+# Renamed rules in ignore comments
+
+The mdtest registry defines `old-rule-name` as an alias for `new-rule-name`. The rule never emits a
+diagnostic, so these examples disable warnings about unused ignore comments.
+
+```toml
+[rules]
+renamed-rule-in-ignore-comment = "warn"
+unused-ignore-comment = "ignore"
+unused-type-ignore-comment = "ignore"
+```
+
+## Line-level ignores
+
+The fix replaces just the ty rule name, preserving its `ty:` prefix and other type checkers' codes.
+
+```py
+# snapshot
+x = 1  # type: ignore[old-rule-name, ty:old-rule-name]  # keep this comment
+```
+
+```snapshot
+warning[renamed-rule-in-ignore-comment]: Rule `old-rule-name` has been renamed to `new-rule-name`
+ --> src/mdtest_snippet.py:2:41
+  |
+2 | x = 1  # type: ignore[old-rule-name, ty:old-rule-name]  # keep this comment
+  |                                         ^^^^^^^^^^^^^
+help: Replace `old-rule-name` with `new-rule-name`
+  |
+1 | # snapshot
+  - x = 1  # type: ignore[old-rule-name, ty:old-rule-name]  # keep this comment
+2 + x = 1  # type: ignore[old-rule-name, ty:new-rule-name]  # keep this comment
+  |
+```
+
+## File-level ignores
+
+```py
+# error: [renamed-rule-in-ignore-comment]
+# ty: ignore[old-rule-name]
+
+x = 1
+```
+
+## Both names in one comment
+
+When a comment already contains the current name, ty reports the rename without offering a fix.
+
+```py
+# snapshot
+x = 1  # ty: ignore[old-rule-name, new-rule-name]
+```
+
+```snapshot
+warning[renamed-rule-in-ignore-comment]: Rule `old-rule-name` has been renamed to `new-rule-name`
+ --> src/mdtest_snippet.py:2:21
+  |
+2 | x = 1  # ty: ignore[old-rule-name, new-rule-name]
+  |                     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^
+```
+
+If the old name suppresses a diagnostic, `unused-type-ignore-comment` can offer to remove the
+current name. Here, `other-tool` separates the two names. A fix that removed the old name would
+touch a different part of the comment, so `--fix` could apply both deletions in one pass and expose
+the diagnostic.
+
+```py
+# snapshot
+y = 2  # type: ignore[ty:new-rule-name, other-tool, ty:old-rule-name]
+```
+
+```snapshot
+warning[renamed-rule-in-ignore-comment]: Rule `old-rule-name` has been renamed to `new-rule-name`
+ --> src/mdtest_snippet.py:4:56
+  |
+4 | y = 2  # type: ignore[ty:new-rule-name, other-tool, ty:old-rule-name]
+  |                                                        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^
+```
+
+## Suppressing the rule
+
+```py
+x = 1  # ty: ignore[old-rule-name, renamed-rule-in-ignore-comment]
+```

+## Shadowing methods
+
+### Explanation and basic examples
+
+Consider the following example where a `method` on a class can be dynamically `swap`ped with another
+method:
+
+```py
+class C:
+    def method(self, x: int) -> str:
+        print("original")
+        return str(x)
+
+    def some_compatible_method(self, x: int) -> str:
+        print("replaced")
+        return str(x)
+
+    def swap(self) -> None:
+        # TODO: this should not be an error
+        # error: [invalid-assignment]
+        self.method = self.some_compatible_method
+
+c = C()
+c.swap()
+```
+
+When `swap` is called, `self.some_compatible_method` creates a bound method object which is assigned
+to the *instance attribute* `self.method`, i.e. it shadows the function defined on the class itself
+(`C.method`). At runtime, when `c.method` is accessed, Python first looks up `method` on the class
+itself. It finds the original function `C.method`, but since it is a non-data descriptor, attribute
+lookup continues to check if there is an attribute on the instance itself (see
+`descriptor_protocol.md` for details). In this case, it finds the bound method object referring to
+`self.some_compatible_method` and returns it *without calling `__get__`*, i.e. the function is not
+bound to the instance "again".
+
+In summary, calling `c.method(42)` works, returns a string, and prints "replaced":
+
+```py
+# TODO: This works at runtime, so we shouldn't emit an error here
+# error: [invalid-argument-type] "Argument to function `C.method` is incorrect: Expected `C`, found `Literal[42]`"
+# error: [missing-argument] "No argument provided for required parameter `x` of function `C.method`"
+reveal_type(c.method(42))  # revealed: str
+```
+
+We can see that `C.method` is not actually replaced, though. Calling `C.method(c, 42)` directly
+still invokes the original function on the class. It prints "original" and returns a string.
+
+```py
+reveal_type(C.method(c, 42))  # revealed: str
+```
+
+Since this is a common pattern to shadow methods on instances of a class this way, ty does supports
+this pattern. We generally allow this replacement if the callable being assigned has a signature
+that is compatible with the original method:
+
+```py
+from typing import Callable
+
+class Correct:
+    def method(self, x: int, /) -> str:
+        return str(x)
+
+    def compatible_method(self, x: int, /) -> str:
+        return str(x)
+
+    def swap(self, replacement: Callable[[int], str]) -> None:
+        # TODO: this should not be an error
+        # error: [invalid-assignment]
+        self.method = self.compatible_method
+
+        # TODO: this should not be an error
+        # error: [invalid-assignment]
+        self.method = replacement
+
+        # TODO: this should not be an error
+        # error: [invalid-assignment]
+        self.method = lambda x: str(x)
+
+        class CompatibleCallable:
+            def __call__(self, x: int) -> str:
+                return str(x)
+
+        # TODO: this should not be an error
+        # error: [invalid-assignment]
+        self.method = CompatibleCallable()

Failing during deserialization isn't ideal. It leads to worse errors over all (this will fail `pyproject.toml` discovery). We should always prefer to deserialize any setting that remotely looks valid and fail/error when building settings instead.

I'll work on a follow up.

> I doubt anybody is using baselines right now,

I don't think this true. But they're experimental, so it's fine to break them
I'm also not sure if we should do these here? Can't we do this at the options merge level?
I don't think we should hard code this here. We should probably inject the registry as we do in other code (or inject the db and get the rule registry from there)

This test would be more robust to future changes if it didn't depend on the fact that only type alias RHS are currently deferred in stub files. Arguably we should always defer all RHS of all assignments in a stub (other type checkers do - see astral-sh/ty#3967), and if we make that change, this test would no longer serve its purpose.

I think we could instead use a standalone subscript in the stub to test this distinction:

```python
from builtins import list as Marker

Marker[Later]

class Later: ...
```

Here `reaching_definitions` should find the later class because inference recognizes `Marker` as a generic class and treats `Later` as a type argument. If we replace the import with `Marker: dict[object, object]`, the same `Marker[Later]` is an eager key lookup and `Later` has no reaching definition.

This would all remain true, even if we fix astral-sh/ty#3967.

body: Yes, this is exactly right, it's just a fast path. I'll clarify the comment.
I'm not sure I understand the point of this branch from the comment, is the idea that if `previous` is `Unknown` we can skip computing `result` and return `Unknown` directly as a fast-path?

Hmm, the synthetic loop header case seems odd. Shouldn't this API ideally resolve synthetic loop headers to their reaching definitions, so a caller never sees them or has to care about them? There is precedent for this already in the dictionary-key completion code.

I consolidated some of these into `provides_candidate_evidence`, but there are some remaining checks that are not entirely principled (some from before this PR). The eventual goal (outlined by https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/3933) is to remove `UnspecializedTypeVar` entirely and propagate outer type variables directly to jointly solve nested generic calls, so I don't think we need to solve that problem in this PR.

I think we could add a test in `deprecated.md` to cover the motivating case for this (whether we actually keep this field or take a different approach). If a module conditionally defines a `@deprecated` function named `len`, a later bare reference like `ref = len` warns on both main and this branch. Checking only the final union with `builtins.len` would currently lose that warning.

But I also think this is pretty heavyweight machinery in a core system, just to support an edge case (deprecation), and I'm not sure it should be needed at all. It seems like it is basically a workaround for `check_deprecated` not handling unions. What if we just fixed that instead?

Could the snapshot carets use source columns for the start and end of the name? `TextRange` is measured in UTF-8 bytes, so on `é = value` the marker starts one column to the right of `value`, and a read of `π` gets two carets. `LineIndex::line_column` already converts both offsets for these cases.
