+## Bounds apply to the matching union member
+
+A type variable's bound applies only to argument members matched to that variable. `Any` nested
+inside another union member does not change which evidence is subject to the bound.
+
+```py
+from typing import Any
+
+def extract[T: int](value: T | list[Any]) -> T:
+    raise NotImplementedError
+
+def check(value: int | list[Any]):
+    reveal_type(extract(value))  # revealed: int
+```
+
+## Invalid members of a bounded union argument
+
+Every member of an argument union must satisfy the parameter type, including any bounds. The call is
+invalid if no member matches, or if only some members match. This covers
+<https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/4277>.
+
+```py
+class Box[T]: ...
+
+def unbox[T: bytes](value: Box[T] | T) -> T:
+    raise NotImplementedError
+
+def invalid_union(value: int | str, partly_valid: Box[bytes] | int):
+    unbox(value)  # error: [invalid-argument-type]
+    unbox(partly_valid)  # error: [invalid-argument-type]
+```
+
+The same check excludes a generic overload whose bound cannot be satisfied, allowing another
+overload to match:
+
+```py
+from typing import overload
+
+@overload
+def select[T: bytes](value: Box[T] | T) -> T: ...
+@overload
+def select(value: int | str) -> bool: ...
+def select(value: object) -> object: ...
+def check_overload(value: int | str):
+    reveal_type(select(value))  # revealed: bool
+```
+
+## Constrained variables shared by union members
+
+All members of an argument union must select the same declared constraint. That constraint also
+determines the result's element type.
+
+```py
+def collect[Text: (str, bytes)](value: Text | list[Text]) -> list[Text]:
+    raise NotImplementedError
+
+def check(value: str | list[str], mixed: str | list[bytes]):
+    result = collect(value)
+    reveal_type(result)  # revealed: list[str]
+    result.append(1)  # error: [invalid-argument-type]
+    collect(mixed)  # error: [invalid-argument-type]
+```
+
+## Concrete union members preserve type variable defaults
+
+Matching a concrete union member contributes no evidence for the type variable. Inference uses the
+variable's default unless another argument determines its type.
+
+```toml
+[environment]
+python-version = "3.13"
+```
+
+```py
+def optional[T = str](value: T | None) -> T:
+    raise NotImplementedError
+
+def with_evidence[T = str](value: T | None, other: T) -> T:
+    return other
+
+reveal_type(optional(None))  # revealed: str
+reveal_type(with_evidence(None, 1))  # revealed: Literal[1]
+```
+
+## Recovery from an invalid union argument
+
+Rejecting an argument union does not discard inference from its valid members. The call retains that
+information in its return type for error recovery.
+
+```py
+def element[T](value: list[T] | str) -> T:
+    raise NotImplementedError
+
+def check(value: list[int] | None):
+    # error: [invalid-argument-type]
+    reveal_type(element(value))  # revealed: int
+```
+
+## Gradual evidence in union arguments
+
+A gradual argument retains its gradual type when matched to the variable member of a union. Concrete
+members of the argument still contribute their own evidence.
+
+```py
+from typing import Any
+
+def optional[T](value: T | None) -> T:
+    raise NotImplementedError
+
+def check(value: Any, mixed: Any | str):
+    reveal_type(optional(value))  # revealed: Any
+    reveal_type(optional(mixed))  # revealed: Any | str
+```
+
+Aliases preserve the same evidence in both the argument and parameter types:
+
+```py
+type OptionalValue[T] = T | None
+type Gradual = Any | str
+
+def aliased_optional[T](value: OptionalValue[T]) -> T:
+    raise NotImplementedError
+
+def check_alias(value: Gradual, static: OptionalValue[str]):
+    reveal_type(aliased_optional(value))  # revealed: Any | str
+    reveal_type(aliased_optional(static))  # revealed: str
+```
+
+A gradual intersection or an `Any` base does not discard the known specialization of another member
+or base:
+
+```py
+from ty_extensions import Intersection
+
+class Source[T]:
+    value: T
+
+class DynamicSource(Source[str], Any): ...
+
+def from_source[T](value: Source[T] | None) -> T:
+    raise NotImplementedError
+
+def check_source(narrowed: Intersection[Any, Source[str]], inherited: DynamicSource):
+    reveal_type(from_source(narrowed))  # revealed: str
+    reveal_type(from_source(inherited))  # revealed: str
+```
+
+## Nested gradual evidence in unions
+
+A gradual type argument remains evidence for a type variable inside a nested union. Inference
+preserves `Any` instead of using the variable's default.
+
+```toml
+[environment]
+python-version = "3.13"
+```
+
+```py
+from typing import Any
+
+class Box[T]:
+    def get(self) -> T:
+        raise NotImplementedError
+
+def unbox[T = str](value: Box[T | None] | int) -> T:
+    raise NotImplementedError
+
+reveal_type(unbox(Box[Any]()))  # revealed: Any
+```
+
+Gradual evidence from a generic base is also preserved, including when that base is nested inside
+another generic argument:
+
+```py
+class AnyBox(Box[Any]): ...
+class WrappedBox(Box[AnyBox]): ...
+
+def nested_unbox[T = str](value: Box[Box[T | None]] | int) -> T:
+    raise NotImplementedError
+
+reveal_type(unbox(AnyBox()))  # revealed: Any
+reveal_type(nested_unbox(Box[AnyBox]()))  # revealed: Any
+reveal_type(nested_unbox(WrappedBox()))  # revealed: Any
+```
+
+Recursively specialized bases still allow a finite result: extracting the element type does not
+require expanding that element's own bases indefinitely.
+
+```py
+class Growing[T](Box["Growing[list[T]]"]): ...
+
+reveal_type(unbox(Growing[int]()))  # revealed: Growing[list[int]]
+```
+
+## Variance when matching union arguments
+
+For a covariant parameter, the inferred type must include the element type of every argument union
+member. The result is the union of those types, regardless of member order.
+
+```py
+from typing import assert_type
+
+class Source[T]:
+    def get(self) -> T:
+        raise NotImplementedError
+
+def from_source[T](value: Source[T] | None) -> T:
+    raise NotImplementedError
+
+def check_source(value: Source[int] | Source[str], reverse: Source[str] | Source[int]):
+    assert_type(from_source(value), int | str)
+    assert_type(from_source(reverse), int | str)
+```
+
+For a contravariant parameter, the inferred type must be accepted by every argument union member.
+Only `Never` satisfies both `int` and `str` consumers.
+
+```py
+class Sink[T]:
+    def put(self, value: T) -> None: ...
+
+def from_sink[T](value: Sink[T] | None) -> T:
+    raise NotImplementedError
+
+def check_sink(value: Sink[int] | Sink[str]):
+    reveal_type(from_sink(value))  # revealed: Never
+```
+
+## Union inference preserves outer type variables
+
+Matching a union preserves an outer type variable's identity. Evidence from another argument can
+select that variable even when the union also permits a less precise specialization.
+
+```py
+class Pair[A, B]:
+    def get(self) -> tuple[A, B]:
+        raise NotImplementedError
+
+def choose[T](value: Pair[T, object] | Pair[object, T], hint: T) -> T:
+    return hint
+
+def forward[U](value: Pair[U, object], hint: U):
+    reveal_type(choose(value, hint))  # revealed: U@forward
+    reveal_type(choose(hint=hint, value=value))  # revealed: U@forward
+```
+
+## Preserving type variables when forwarding a generic union
+
+Forwarding a union to a helper with the same parameter type preserves the caller's type variable. A
+broader alternative specialization does not widen the return type: the result must satisfy every
+valid specialization. This example is reduced from Werkzeug.
+
+```py

+    value: V  # invariant
+
+def first_value[V](mapping: V | Batch[V]) -> V:
+    raise NotImplementedError
+
+class MultiDict[V]:
+    def add(self, value: V): ...
+    def extend_values(self, mapping: V | Batch[V]):
+        self.add(first_value(mapping))  # no diagnostic
+```
+
+## Unions nested in covariant type arguments
+
+Constraints on a nested union are solved together with constraints from other arguments. The call is
+valid if an assignment satisfies both, even when a type variable defaults to `Never`.
+
+```toml
+[environment]
+python-version = "3.13"
+```

+# `no-method-argument` (`PLE0211`)
+
+```toml
+lint.preview = true
+lint.select = ["PLE0211"]
+```
+
+## Instance and class methods
+
+A bound method receives an instance or class as an implicit positional argument.
+
+```py
+class Example:
+    def method():  # snapshot: no-method-argument
+        return 1
+
+    @classmethod
+    def class_method():  # error: [no-method-argument]
+        return 1
+
+    async def async_method():  # error: [no-method-argument]
+        return 1
+```
+
+```snapshot
+error[PLE0211]: Method `method` has no parameter for its implicit argument
+ --> src/mdtest_snippet.py:2:9
+  |
+2 |     def method():  # snapshot: no-method-argument
+  |         ^^^^^^
+```
+
+## Functions and methods that accept a receiver
+
+Static methods and functions outside a class do not receive an implicit argument.
+A positional parameter or `*args` can receive the implicit argument of a method.
+
+```py
+def function():  # no diagnostic
+    return 1
+
+class Example:
+    @staticmethod
+    def static_method():  # no diagnostic
+        return 1
+
+    def method(self):  # no diagnostic
+        def inner():  # no diagnostic
+            return 1
+        return inner()
+
+    def positional_only(self, /):  # no diagnostic
+        return 1
+
+    def variadic(*args):  # no diagnostic
+        return 1
+
+    @classmethod
+    def class_method(cls):  # no diagnostic
+        return 1
+
+    @classmethod
+    def variadic_class_method(*args):  # no diagnostic
+        return 1
+```
+
+## Keyword-only parameters
+
+Keyword-only parameters cannot receive a positional receiver. For compatibility
+with Pylint's E0211, `**kwargs` is exempt even though it cannot receive one either.
+
+```py
+class Example:
+    def keyword_only(*, self):  # error: [no-method-argument]
+        return 1
+
+    @classmethod
+    def keyword_only_class_method(*, cls):  # error: [no-method-argument]
+        return 1
+
+    def kwargs_only(**kwargs):  # no diagnostic
+        return 1
+
+    def variadic(*args, keyword=None):  # no diagnostic
+        return 1
+```
+
+## Special methods
+
+`__new__` receives the class explicitly from Python's constructor machinery.
+`__init_subclass__` and `__class_getitem__` are implicitly class methods.
+
+```py
+class Example:
+    def __new__():  # error: [no-method-argument]
+        return object.__new__(Example)
+
+    def __init__():  # error: [no-method-argument]
+        pass
+
+    def __init_subclass__():  # error: [no-method-argument]
+        pass
+
+    def __class_getitem__():  # error: [no-method-argument]
+        return 1
+
+class Meta(type):
+    def method():  # error: [no-method-argument]
+        return 1
+
+class ExplicitStaticNew:
+    @staticmethod
+    def __new__():  # error: [no-method-argument]
+        return object.__new__(ExplicitStaticNew)
+
+class ExplicitStaticInitSubclass:
+    @staticmethod
+    def __init_subclass__():  # no diagnostic
+        pass
+```
+
+## Intentional class-only calls
+
+A function accessed directly on the class can be called without an instance.
+The rule still flags its definition because calling it through an instance fails.
+An explicit `staticmethod` or a suppression can express that this is intentional.
+
+```py
+class Example:
+    def method():  # error: [no-method-argument]
+        return 1
+
+    def intentional():  # noqa: PLE0211
+        return 1
+
+Example.method()
+Example.intentional()
+```
+
+## Naming rules are independent
+
+```toml
+lint.select = ["N804", "N805"]
+```
+
+Selecting naming rules alone does not enable the missing-argument check.
+
+```py
+class Example:
+    def method():  # no diagnostic
+        return 1
+
+    @classmethod
+    def class_method():  # no diagnostic
+        return 1
+
+    def wrong_name(this):  # error: [invalid-first-argument-name-for-method]
+        return 1
+
+    @classmethod
+    def wrong_class_name(self):  # error: [invalid-first-argument-name-for-class-method]
+        return 1
+```
+
+## Custom method decorators
+
+```toml
+lint.preview = true
+lint.select = ["PLE0211"]
+lint.pep8-naming.staticmethod-decorators = ["example.static"]
+lint.pep8-naming.classmethod-decorators = ["example.class_method"]
+```

+use crate::Violation;
+use crate::checkers::ast::Checker;
+use crate::codes::Category;
+
+/// ## What it does
+/// Checks for methods that have no parameter to receive their implicit argument.
+///
+/// ## Why is this bad?
+/// Calling a method through an instance passes the instance as an implicit
+/// positional argument. Class methods receive the class instead. A method without a
+/// positional parameter or `*args` cannot accept this argument and raises a
+/// `TypeError` when called this way.
+///
+/// Add an instance or class parameter, conventionally named `self` or `cls`.
+/// If the function does not need either, use `@staticmethod` instead.
+///
+/// ## Example
+/// ```python
+/// class Example:
+///     def method():
+///         return 1
+/// ```
+///
+/// Use instead:
+/// ```python
+/// class Example:
+///     def method(self):
+///         return 1
+/// ```
+///
+/// ## Known problems
+/// An ordinary function defined in a class can be called directly through the
+/// class, without passing an instance: `Example.method()` works in the example
+/// above, while `Example().method()` raises a `TypeError`. This rule flags the
+/// definition regardless of how it is called. Use `@staticmethod`, or suppress
+/// the diagnostic if class-only access is intentional.
+///
+/// Custom decorators can change whether a method receives an implicit argument.
+/// Decorators that make a method static can be configured using
+/// [`lint.pep8-naming.staticmethod-decorators`].
+///
+/// For compatibility with Pylint's E0211, methods accepting `**kwargs` are
+/// exempt, even though `**kwargs` cannot receive a positional argument.
+///
+/// ## Options
+/// - `lint.pep8-naming.classmethod-decorators`
+/// - `lint.pep8-naming.staticmethod-decorators`
+///
+/// ## References
+/// - [Python documentation: Instance methods](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/datamodel.html#instance-methods)
+#[derive(ViolationMetadata)]
+#[violation_metadata(preview_since = "NEXT_RUFF_VERSION", category = Category::Suspicious)]
+pub(crate) struct NoMethodArgument {
+    method_name: String,
+}
+
+impl Violation for NoMethodArgument {
+    #[derive_message_formats]
+    fn message(&self) -> String {
+        let Self { method_name } = self;
+        format!("Method `{method_name}` has no parameter for its implicit argument")
+    }
+}
+
+/// PLE0211
+pub(crate) fn no_method_argument(checker: &Checker, scope: &Scope) {
+    let Some(function) = scope.kind.as_function() else {
+        return;
+    };
+
+    let parameters = &function.parameters;
+    if !parameters.posonlyargs.is_empty()
+        || !parameters.args.is_empty()
+        || parameters.vararg.is_some()
+        || parameters.kwarg.is_some()

+## Abstract models
+
+### Basic
+
+An abstract model provides reusable fields without creating its own database table. Its concrete
+subclasses receive an integer primary key unless they declare or inherit an explicit primary key.
+
+```py
+from django.db import models
+
+class AbstractBook(models.Model):
+    title = models.CharField(max_length=200)
+
+    class Meta:
+        abstract = True
+
+class Ebook(AbstractBook):
+    file_size = models.IntegerField()
+
+class Book(AbstractBook):
+    isbn = models.CharField(max_length=13, primary_key=True)
+
+def _(abstract: AbstractBook, ebook: Ebook, book: Book):
+    # Abstract models do not have an automatic primary key.
+    abstract.id  # error: [unresolved-attribute]
+
+    # Concrete models without an explicit primary key have an automatic integer key.
+    reveal_type(ebook.id)  # revealed: int
+    reveal_type(ebook.pk)  # revealed: int
+    reveal_type(ebook.title)  # revealed: str
+    reveal_type(ebook.file_size)  # revealed: int
+
+    # The explicit ISBN primary key prevents an automatic `id`.
+    book.id  # error: [unresolved-attribute]
+    reveal_type(book.pk)  # revealed: str
+    reveal_type(book.title)  # revealed: str
+    reveal_type(book.isbn)  # revealed: str
+```
+
+### Multiple inheritance
+
+An abstract base without a primary key does not shadow an inherited `id`, regardless of the base
+class order. Regression test for <https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/4822>.
+
+```py
+from uuid import uuid4
+from django.db import models
+
+class AbstractHasTitle(models.Model):
+    title = models.CharField(max_length=200)
+
+    class Meta:
+        abstract = True
+
+class AbstractHasId(models.Model):
+    id = models.UUIDField(primary_key=True, default=uuid4)
+
+    class Meta:
+        abstract = True
+
+# Django allows separate `Meta` configurations, but ty currently reports a conflict between them.
+# error: [invalid-attribute-override]

+//! Loads, matches, and writes diagnostic baselines.
+//!
+//! Baselines let you adopt ty or enable a new rule without first fixing every existing error or
+//! adding individual suppression comments. A baseline records those errors in a project-wide JSON
+//! file, so you can focus on new diagnostics while working through the old ones over time.
+//! Only lint diagnostics can go in the baseline. Other diagnostics, such as syntax errors and
+//! messages from `reveal_type`, still appear.

body: I don't know about this. It bakes in assumptions about Salsa that might change.

We could return the gradual callable `(...) -> Unknown` here, no? And that would be somewhat more precise than just `Unknown`; it would at least reject arbitrary attributes that `Callable` does not promise.

I think it would be useful to a future reader here to explain the asymmetry: why do we represent intersections here but not unions? Maybe something like this (you could also link to my longer comment, though I don't love relying on links to GitHub comments for important explanations), inserted between the two existing paragraphs here:

> An intersection of callables describes a callable supporting every constituent signature, so it accurately represents a conjunction of upper bounds on a ParamSpec. A union of callables describes alternative callable types rather than their shared calling interface, so it's not an accurate representation of a conjunction of lower bounds on a ParamSpec. 

> For example, callbacks accepting `(int, object)` and `(object, int)` share the calling interface `(int, int)`. A callable accepting only two integers satisfies that shared interface but satisfies neither original callable type, so `(int, int)` does not belong to the union `(int, object) | (object, int)`. Supporting conjunctions of lower bounds on a `ParamSpec` requires constructing a common signature (e.g. constructing `(int, int)` from the conjunction of `(object, int)` and `(int, object)`); until we implement that, union-valued solutions are rejected.

body: With the bitset `ConstraintProvenance`, I'm not convinced this nested-allocation layout makes sense, with up to seven entries for every possible combination of bits. Codex ran some tests and reported that ~90% of upper bounds have 0 or 1 clauses, which strongly favors simplifying this to an `FxOrderSet<(ConstraintProvenance, Type)>` instead -- that keeps hashed deduplication but avoids nested double container allocation. I think that version also simplifies the readers considerably.

Kind of mentioned below, but I'm not sure it makes sense to have a method like this that is used only when there is declared context. Our "choose a compatible specialization" logic should be more generalized than that.

I think we need to rebase this PR on top of (now merged) #28303 in order to better understand how this interacts with the logic in that PR. If that rebase is done naively I think the "choose the first specialization that works" logic here will cause us to lose precision relative to main in cases where #28303 would be able to intersect the multiple alternatives -- but only if there is return context, which is kind of weird. I think the right integration of the two is that we should check the #28303 merged specialization first and use that if it works, then check the merged specialization and use that if it works, and only then go through the single options and pick one?

It's still not really clear to me that it makes sense to use this "pick one" logic specifically only if there is return context. There are also cases where the merged specialization just fails the call entirely (even without return context, because it makes the argument checks fail), and we'd be better off picking one specialization that works. So I think this logic maybe should be applied more broadly than just when there is return context.

This is a bit confusing because "evidence" is no longer part of the bitset. I think it would be clearer here to describe both inferred and declared bounds upfront, and then note that we call both of these evidence bounds.

That would also prevent us from accidentally checking a candidate with a different `inferable` set than the one we used to compute it.

If that noticeably grows the cached results, we could instead store it once on `CandidateSolutions::Constrained`, and give callbacks a borrowed view that pairs the bounds with the set.

It wouldn't need to capture the set from outside the closure, but it would still have to pass it to `bounds.solve` or `bounds.accepts_candidate`. +## Bottom callable assignability
+
+The bottom callable accepts every argument list and returns `Never`, so it can satisfy any callable
+signature, including one with required keyword-only parameters. Returning `Never` alone is not
+sufficient, nor is accepting every argument list with an incompatible return type.
+
+```py
+from typing import Any, Callable, Never, Protocol
+from ty_extensions import Bottom
+
+class Required(Protocol):
+    def __call__(self, value: int, /, *, enabled: bool) -> str: ...
+
+def never_returns(*values: object, **options: object) -> Never:
+    raise NotImplementedError
+
+def check(
+    bottom: Bottom[Callable[..., Any]],
+    restricted: Callable[[int], Never],
+    returns_none: Bottom[Callable[..., None]],
+) -> None:
+    positional: Callable[[str, bytes], int] = bottom  # no diagnostic
+    keyword_only: Required = bottom  # no diagnostic
+    declared: Required = never_returns  # no diagnostic
+
+    wrong_parameters: Callable[[str], int] = restricted  # error: [invalid-assignment]
+    wrong_return: Callable[[int], str] = returns_none  # error: [invalid-assignment]
+```
+
+Receiver restrictions still apply when a bound method accepts every argument list and returns
+`Never`.
+
+```py
+class Restricted:
+    def method(self: "Allowed", *values: object, **options: object) -> Never:
+        raise NotImplementedError
+
+class Allowed(Restricted): ...
+
+def check_receiver(restricted: Restricted, allowed: Allowed) -> None:
+    valid: Callable[[int], str] = allowed.method  # no diagnostic
+    invalid: Callable[[int], str] = restricted.method  # error: [invalid-assignment]
+```
+
+## Top callable assignability
+
+Every callable is assignable to the top callable, which permits no calls and has return type
+`object`. A narrower return type or a parameter list that permits calls still imposes requirements.
+
+```py
+from typing import Callable, Protocol
+from ty_extensions import Top
+
+class Required(Protocol):
+    def __call__(self, *, enabled: bool) -> bytes: ...
+
+def check(positional: Callable[[int], str], keyword_only: Required) -> None:
+    first: Top[Callable[..., object]] = positional  # no diagnostic
+    second: Top[Callable[..., object]] = keyword_only  # no diagnostic
+    wrong_return: Top[Callable[..., int]] = positional  # error: [invalid-assignment]
+    wrong_parameters: Top[Callable[[str], object]] = positional  # error: [invalid-assignment]
+```
+
+A receiver restriction does not prevent assignment to the top callable, since it permits no calls.
+The restriction still applies when assigning to a callable that permits calls.

Removing `remove_seen_paramspecs` here exposes a loss of graduality when an `Any` has been narrowed by `callable()`. With `analysis.strict-generic-narrowing = true`:

```python
from typing import Any, Callable, reveal_type

def capture[**P](f: Callable[P, object]) -> Callable[P, object]:
    return f

def example(f: Any) -> None:
    if callable(f):
        f()  # accepted on both revisions
        captured = capture(f)
        reveal_type(captured)
        captured()
```

On the base, `captured` is `(...) -> object` and the call is accepted. On this PR it becomes `Top[(...) -> object]`, and the call emits `call-top-callable`. Forwarding through a `*args: P.args, **kwargs: P.kwargs` helper has the same regression; this matches the three new `discord.py` errors in the ecosystem report.

The existing gradual-intersection compatibility path infers separately from the `Any` and `Top` positives. Both callable comparisons reach `record_constraint_set` through `infer_from_callable_signature` and `infer_from_constraint_set`. With the filtering removed, both parameter-list bounds enter `pending`, and the combined inference loses the gradual behavior.

Could we preserve graduality when that fallback combines evidence from a single intersection argument, while retaining the new support for repeated ParamSpecs?
I wonder if we could also add this useful typing-spec link to the `Number = 1 + 2` snapshot example up on line 2334?

+//! Loads, matches, and writes diagnostic baselines.
+//!
+//! Baselines let a project adopt ty without first fixing or suppressing every existing error.
+//! By recording those errors, a baseline lets you focus on new ones as you work on the code.
+//! The same approach is useful when enabling a new rule in an existing project.
+//!
+//! The diagnostics are stored in a project-wide JSON file. Those matched by the baseline are
+//! demoted to [`Severity::Hint`]. The CLI hides them, while the LSP keeps them visible to encourage
+//! fixing them or acknowledging them with a suppression comment.
+//!
+//! Like suppression comments, baselines can only suppress lint diagnostics.
+//! Syntax errors and diagnostics such as `reveal_type` cannot be suppressed this way.
+//!
+//! Inline suppression comments such as `# ty: ignore[invalid-assignment]` take precedence over
+//! the baseline. If you add one for a baselined diagnostic, the next baseline update removes
+//! that entry: the comment now suppresses it.
+//!
+//! # Recognizing an existing diagnostic
+//!
+//! The tricky part is recognizing the same error as the code evolves. Adding an import, for
+//! example, shifts this assignment error down by two lines without fixing it:
+//!
+//! ```diff
+//! +import logging
+//! +
+//!  def get_name() -> str: ...
+//!
+//!  name: int = get_name()
+//! ```
+//!
+//! To recognize errors across edits, we use two source-text anchors: the code leading up to the
+//! error and the code starting at the error itself. A diagnostic matches a baseline entry with the
+//! same file and rule if either anchor's normalized text matches, allowing code on the other side to change. This
+//! heuristic is inspired by the [two-hash approach][paper] described in section III-C.
+//!
+//! This lets us recognize existing errors after:
+//!
+//! - Adding or removing lines before the error.
+//! - Changing spacing, or indenting or dedenting a block.
+//! - Moving or reordering blocks within the same file.
+//! - Editing nearby code on one side of the error while the other side stays unchanged.
+//! - Editing code outside the hashed context.
+//! - Switching between LF, CRLF, and CR line endings.
+//!
+//! Ideally, a baseline would also follow an error when its file is renamed or the code moves to
+//! another file. Our heuristic only matches within a file, so these changes require updating the
+//! baseline.
+//!
+//! # Context hashes
+//!
+//! The two anchors are windows of source text: one extends backward, the other forward.
+//! Both include the word containing the start of the primary range, so they overlap on `get_name` here.
+//! The two windows cover the following source text:
+//!
+//! ```text
+//!    name: int = get_name()
+//!                ^^^^^^^^^^     primary range
+//! ...name: int = get_name        preceding window, read backward
+//!                get_name()...  following window, read forward
+//! ```
+//!
+//! We take up to 100 characters (Unicode scalar values) in each direction, stopping at
+//! file boundaries. This keeps enough context to distinguish similar errors without depending on too
+//! much nearby code. In Home Assistant trials, shorter windows confused similar diagnostics;
+//! larger token windows resurfaced more existing diagnostics in Home Assistant and Airflow.
+//!
+//! We ignore spaces and indentation so that changing spacing or reindenting a block preserves its
+//! anchors. Line breaks are retained because they can affect Python semantics, but LF, CRLF, and CR
+//! all become `\n` so that changing line endings also preserves matches (e.g. because of git's auto newline handling).
+//! The character limit applies after this normalization. We don't lex the source, so harmless line breaks inside parentheses
+//! are kept too, and rewrapping a call can change its hash.
+//!
+//! Each anchor is stored as a hash to keep the baseline compact, rather than storing the source text.\
+//! Either hash is enough for a match. Adding the import above leaves the following hash unchanged;
+//! editing code after the call can leave the preceding hash unchanged. Changing `get_name` to
+//! `get_count`, however, changes both hashes. This prevents a different call from matching just
+//! because the preceding code stayed the same, at the cost of also reporting harmless renames again.
+//!
+//! # Reordering and duplicates
+//!
+//! Moving code within a file should not require updating the baseline if its hashes still match.
+//! We process diagnostics in source order, giving each the first unused matching entry:
+//!
+//! ```text
+//! baseline    current    result, where A and B have distinct matching fingerprints
+//! A, B        B, A       both still match
+//! A           A, A       only one matches
+//! ```
+//!
+//! Using each entry only once prevents it from hiding extra occurrences. If two diagnostics have
+//! identical fingerprints, though, we cannot tell which is the old one.
+//!
+//! # Format versions
+//!
+//! Baseline support is experimental and uses format version 0, which may change between ty releases.
+//! We will bump the format version to 1 when promoting the feature to stable. From then on, ty must
+//! be able to read and match baselines written by the previous ty version. Updating a baseline
+//! may always write the current format.
+//!
+//! [paper]: https://codeql.github.com/publications/tracking-analysis-violations.pdf
+
+use std::collections::BTreeMap;
+use std::fmt;
+use std::hash::Hasher;
+
+use anyhow::Context;
+use compact_str::CompactString;
+use ruff_db::diagnostic::{Annotation, Diagnostic, DiagnosticId, LintName, Severity, Span};
+use ruff_db::files::{File, FilePath, system_path_to_file};
+use ruff_db::source::source_text;
+use ruff_db::system::{SystemPath, SystemPathBuf};
+use ruff_text_size::{TextRange, TextSize};
+use rustc_hash::FxHashMap;
+use rustc_stable_hash::{FromStableHash, SipHasher128Hash, StableSipHasher128};
+use serde::de::{self, Visitor};
+use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
+
+use crate::Db;
+
+const BASELINE_VERSION: u32 = 0;
+const CONTEXT_SIZE: usize = 100;
+
+/// Returns a diagnostic if the configured baseline cannot be loaded.
+pub(crate) fn settings_diagnostic(db: &dyn Db) -> Option<Diagnostic> {
+    db.project().settings(db).baseline()?;
+    baselines(db).err().map(Error::to_diagnostic)
+}
+
+/// Demotes matched diagnostics to hints and adds a note identifying the baseline.
+pub(crate) fn demote_diagnostics(db: &dyn Db, file: File, diagnostics: &mut [Diagnostic]) {
+    let project = db.project();
+    let Some(baseline_path) = project.settings(db).baseline() else {
+        return;
+    };
+    let Some(baseline_entries) = baseline(db, file) else {
+        return;
+    };
+    let baseline_path = baseline_path
+        .strip_prefix(project.root(db))
+        .unwrap_or(baseline_path);
+
+    let source = source_text(db, file);
+    let mut entries: Vec<_> = diagnostics
+        .iter()
+        .enumerate()
+        .filter_map(|(index, diagnostic)| {
+            let diagnostic = BaselineDiagnostic::from_diagnostic(diagnostic)?;
+            Some((index, diagnostic.entry(source.as_str())))
+        })
+        .collect();
+    entries.sort_by(|(_, left), (_, right)| left.cmp(right));
+
+    let mut matcher = BaselineMatcher::new(baseline_entries);
+    for (index, entry) in entries {
+        if matcher.consume(&entry) {
+            let diagnostic = &mut diagnostics[index];
+            diagnostic.set_severity(Severity::Hint);
+            diagnostic.info(format_args!("Suppressed by baseline `{baseline_path}`"));
+        }
+    }
+}
+
+pub struct WriteResult {
+    /// The number of diagnostics written to the baseline.
+    pub count: usize,
+    /// The diagnostics that could not be baselined.
+    pub diagnostics: Vec<Diagnostic>,
+}
+
+/// Writes a new baseline containing all eligible diagnostics.
+///
+/// Returns how many diagnostics were baselined and the remaining diagnostics.
+pub fn write(
+    db: &dyn Db,
+    path: &SystemPath,
+    mut diagnostics: Vec<Diagnostic>,
+) -> anyhow::Result<WriteResult> {
+    let count = BaselineFile::extract_from_diagnostics(db, &mut diagnostics).write(db, path)?;
+    // Errors from loading the old baseline no longer apply after a successful write.
+    diagnostics.retain(|diagnostic| diagnostic.id() != DiagnosticId::InvalidBaseline);

body: this is getting a bit ridiculous, but I think it's a valuable optimization

This actually surfaced something pretty interesting about this PR, which is that it is kind of making our generic inference more clever than what our assignability checking can handle. In general our union assignability/subtype checking suffers from the problem that we can't detect cases where neither arm of a union is independently a super-type of some other type, but collectively they are. This is tracked in https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/216.

This PR creates those cases, because it creates types like `(U & ~str) | str`, which we can't inherently recognize as assignable from `U`.

The previous PR in the stack solves this by implementing the general union simplification `(U & ~str) | str -> U | str`, which again allows us to recognize that `U` is assignable to this type.

The top materialization fix here started creating types like `(U & ~Top[A]) | A`, which that union simplification does not (and should not) simplify, so we started failing calls due to not realizing that `U` should be assignable to this type.

This PR now fixes that with an extra fallback case in assignability-to-a-union, which is a bit ugly but not too bad, so I went ahead with it.

+### Fixed outer variables in unions
+
+TODO: After #29236 lands, simplify these tests to use direct union annotations instead of `Callable`
+types, which are currently needed to exercise the full constraints.
+
+A caller's type variable contributes to the inferred return type even when the callee's type also
+accepts a concrete union member:
+
+```py
+from collections.abc import Callable
+
+def helper[T](value: Callable[[], T | int]) -> T:
+    raise NotImplementedError
+
+def outer[U](value: Callable[[], U | str]) -> None:
+    reveal_type(helper(value))  # revealed: (U@outer & ~int) | str
+```
+
+A disjoint bound also preserves the caller's variable. When the variable's entire bound fits the
+concrete `int` member, only the remaining `str` member contributes to inference:
+
+```py
+def disjoint[U: bytes](value: Callable[[], U | str]) -> None:
+    reveal_type(helper(value))  # revealed: U@disjoint | str
+
+def covered[U: int](value: Callable[[], U | str]) -> None:
+    reveal_type(helper(value))  # revealed: str
+```
+
+The caller's variable also supplies inference evidence without a separate union member:
+
+```py
+def only_outer[U: str](value: Callable[[], U]) -> None:
+    reveal_type(helper(value))  # revealed: U@only_outer
+```
+
+A literal union member excludes only that literal from the caller's contribution:
+
+```py
+from typing import Literal
+
+def helper_literal[T](value: Callable[[], T | Literal[1]]) -> T:
+    raise NotImplementedError
+
+def outer_literal[U](value: Callable[[], U | str]) -> None:
+    reveal_type(helper_literal(value))  # revealed: (U@outer_literal & ~Literal[1]) | str
+```
+
+### Fully covered outer variables in unions
+
+When the concrete union member covers the caller's entire variable, it contributes no inference
+evidence. We use the callee's default, or `Unknown` if there is none.
+
+```toml
+[environment]
+python-version = "3.13"
+```
+
+```py
+from collections.abc import Callable
+
+def helper[T](value: Callable[[], T | int]) -> T:
+    raise NotImplementedError
+
+def defaulted[T = str](value: Callable[[], T | int]) -> T:
+    raise NotImplementedError
+
+def covered[U: int](value: Callable[[], U]):
+    reveal_type(helper(value))  # revealed: Unknown
+    result = defaulted(value)
+    reveal_type(result)  # revealed: str
+```
+
+### Invariant arguments with unions
+
+When a union annotation contains two inferred variables (e.g. `T | V`), invariant arguments can
+determine which variable accepts each union member:
+
+```py
+from collections.abc import Callable
+
+def helper[T, V](value: Callable[[], T | V], first: list[T], second: list[V]) -> tuple[T, V]:
+    raise NotImplementedError
+
+def outer[U](value: Callable[[], U | str], variables: list[U], strings: list[str]) -> None:
+    reveal_type(helper(value, variables, strings))  # revealed: tuple[U@outer, str]
+    reveal_type(helper(value, strings, variables))  # revealed: tuple[str, U@outer]
+```
+
+### Bounds and constraints with fixed outer union members
+
+In a union annotation like `T | int`, the concrete part (`int` here) can accept part of the caller's
+type variable. The remaining part must satisfy the callee's bound or constraints; requiring the
+entire caller variable to satisfy them would reject these valid calls:
+
+```py
+from collections.abc import Callable
+
+def bounded[T: str](value: Callable[[], T | int]) -> T:
+    raise NotImplementedError
+
+def constrained[T: (str, bytes)](value: Callable[[], T | int]) -> T:
+    raise NotImplementedError
+
+def split_constraints[U: (int, str)](value: Callable[[], U | str]) -> None:
+    reveal_type(bounded(value))  # revealed: str
+    reveal_type(constrained(value))  # revealed: str
+```
+
+Without a separate `str` member, the inferred bound preserves the caller's variable while excluding
+its `int` part. A constrained callee instead selects the compatible declared constraint:
+
+```py
+def only_bound[U: int | str](value: Callable[[], U]) -> None:
+    reveal_type(bounded(value))  # revealed: U@only_bound & ~int
+    reveal_type(constrained(value))  # revealed: str
+```
+
+The caller's variable remains fixed. An unrestricted variable, or one permitting an incompatible
+type, cannot be specialized just to make the call succeed:
+
+```py
+def invalid_bound[U](value: Callable[[], U | str]) -> None:
+    bounded(value)  # error: [invalid-argument-type]
+
+def invalid_constraints[U: (int, complex)](value: Callable[[], U | str]) -> None:
+    constrained(value)  # error: [invalid-argument-type]
+```
+
+### Gradual types in union arms
+
+When matching the caller's `U` against `T | A`, a fully static `A` lets us infer `T` from the part
+of `U` that `A` does not cover: `U & ~A`. We cannot apply this subtraction when `A` contains `Any`,
+because gradual assignability does not treat `Any` as a single fixed type.

I think the reverse direction is also true, so this is an equivalence. But I understand that we are interested in that specific direction here.

This part is not clear to me. I don't understand the "because gradual assignability does not treat `Any` as a single fixed type" justification. It seems like the `U ≤ T | A   =>   U & ~A ≤ T` implication should hold for gradual types as well. Was this gradual-type exemption implemented to avoid seemingly-superfluous union elements like `U & ~tuple[list[Any]]`?

Would it make sense to subtract the top-materialization of the gradual type instead? This should lead to the same results here (because `U & ~Top[tuple[list[Any]]] = Never` if `U: tuple[list[int]]`).

An example where this is relevant would be (thank you Codex):
```py
def f[T](x: Callable[[], T | list[Any]]) -> T:
    raise NotImplementedError

def g[U: int](x: Callable[[], U | str]) -> None:
    reveal_type(f(x))  # invalid-argument-type, str
```

Inference creates two constraints here
```
U   ≤ T | list[Any]
str ≤ T | list[Any]
```

The second one is easy and will be simplified to `str ≤ T`.

The first one is what this PR targets. However, due to your gradual type exemption, this is currently skipped. This leaves only `str ≤ T`, resulting in `T = str`, which is not an actual solution, resulting in the `invalid-argument-type` error.

If we would allow gradual types instead, we could derive `U & ~Top[list[Any]] ≤ T` from the `U ≤ T | list[Any]` constraint. Since `U` is disjoint from `Top[list[Any]]` (it has an `int` bound), that would result in a `U ≤ T` constraint. Combined with the `str ≤ T` constraint, that would lead to a `T = U | str` solution which could satisfy this call.

+A caller's type variable contributes to the inferred return type even when the callee's type also
+accepts a concrete union member:
+
+```py
+from collections.abc import Callable
+
+def helper[T](value: Callable[[], T | int]) -> T:
+    raise NotImplementedError
+
+def outer[U](value: Callable[[], U | str]) -> None:
+    reveal_type(helper(value))  # revealed: (U@outer & ~int) | str
+```
+
+A disjoint bound also preserves the caller's variable. When the variable's entire bound fits the
+concrete `int` member, only the remaining `str` member contributes to inference:
+
+```py
+def disjoint[U: bytes](value: Callable[[], U | str]) -> None:
+    reveal_type(helper(value))  # revealed: U@disjoint | str
+
+def covered[U: int](value: Callable[[], U | str]) -> None:
+    reveal_type(helper(value))  # revealed: str
+```
+
+The caller's variable also supplies inference evidence without a separate union member:
+
+```py
+def only_outer[U: str](value: Callable[[], U]) -> None:
+    reveal_type(helper(value))  # revealed: U@only_outer
+```
+
+A literal union member excludes only that literal from the caller's contribution:
+
+```py
+from typing import Literal
+
+def helper_literal[T](value: Callable[[], T | Literal[1]]) -> T:
+    raise NotImplementedError
+
+def outer_literal[U](value: Callable[[], U | str]) -> None:
+    reveal_type(helper_literal(value))  # revealed: (U@outer_literal & ~Literal[1]) | str
+```
+
+### Fully covered outer variables in unions
+
+When the concrete union member covers the caller's entire variable, it contributes no inference
+evidence. We use the callee's default, or `Unknown` if there is none.
+
+```toml
+[environment]
+python-version = "3.13"
+```
+
+```py
+from collections.abc import Callable
+
+def helper[T](value: Callable[[], T | int]) -> T:
+    raise NotImplementedError
+
+def defaulted[T = str](value: Callable[[], T | int]) -> T:
+    raise NotImplementedError
+
+def covered[U: int](value: Callable[[], U]):
+    reveal_type(helper(value))  # revealed: Unknown
+    result = defaulted(value)
+    reveal_type(result)  # revealed: str
+```
+
+### Invariant arguments with unions
+
+When a union annotation contains two inferred variables (e.g. `T | V`), invariant arguments can
+determine which variable accepts each union member:
+
+```py
+from collections.abc import Callable
+
+def helper[T, V](value: Callable[[], T | V], first: list[T], second: list[V]) -> tuple[T, V]:
+    raise NotImplementedError
+
+def outer[U](value: Callable[[], U | str], variables: list[U], strings: list[str]) -> None:
+    reveal_type(helper(value, variables, strings))  # revealed: tuple[U@outer, str]
+    reveal_type(helper(value, strings, variables))  # revealed: tuple[str, U@outer]
+```
+
+### Bounds and constraints with fixed outer union members
+
+In a union annotation like `T | int`, the concrete part (`int` here) can accept part of the caller's
+type variable. The remaining part must satisfy the callee's bound or constraints; requiring the
+entire caller variable to satisfy them would reject these valid calls:
+
+```py
+from collections.abc import Callable
+
+def bounded[T: str](value: Callable[[], T | int]) -> T:
+    raise NotImplementedError
+
+def constrained[T: (str, bytes)](value: Callable[[], T | int]) -> T:
+    raise NotImplementedError
+
+def split_constraints[U: (int, str)](value: Callable[[], U | str]) -> None:
+    reveal_type(bounded(value))  # revealed: str
+    reveal_type(constrained(value))  # revealed: str
+```
+
+Without a separate `str` member, the inferred bound preserves the caller's variable while excluding
+its `int` part. A constrained callee instead selects the compatible declared constraint:
+
+```py
+def only_bound[U: int | str](value: Callable[[], U]) -> None:
+    reveal_type(bounded(value))  # revealed: U@only_bound & ~int
+    reveal_type(constrained(value))  # revealed: str
+```
+
+The caller's variable remains fixed. An unrestricted variable, or one permitting an incompatible
+type, cannot be specialized just to make the call succeed:
+
+```py
+def invalid_bound[U](value: Callable[[], U | str]) -> None:
+    bounded(value)  # error: [invalid-argument-type]
+
+def invalid_constraints[U: (int, complex)](value: Callable[[], U | str]) -> None:
+    constrained(value)  # error: [invalid-argument-type]
+```
+
+### Gradual types in union arms
+
+When matching the caller's `U` against `T | A`, a fully static `A` lets us infer `T` from the part
+of `U` that `A` does not cover: `U & ~A`. We cannot apply this subtraction when `A` contains `Any`,
+because gradual assignability does not treat `Any` as a single fixed type.

Small edge case: should we respect a literal `name=` override before falling back to the assignment name?

```python
class Article(models.Model):
    status = models.CharField(
        name="state", max_length=1, choices=[("D", "Draft")]
    )
```

[Django's field implementation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/django/django/stable/5.2.x/django/db/models/fields/__init__.py) uses the effective field name when generating the method, so this model gets `get_state_display`. The PR instead accepts `get_status_display()` and reports `get_state_display()` as unresolved. Renamed field attributes already have limitations in our Django support, so this could also just be a TODO.

Should we expose these generated names through `all_members` as well, so it is supported by autocomplete? For the model in the new test, `article.get_status_display()` now resolves, but `ty_extensions._internal.has_member(article, "get_status_display")` still reveals `Literal[False]`.

This might be fine given that it's pre-existing. But I was wondering if we should use the rule's default severity here: ----

Yes. Standard SARIF puts the rule’s default severity in defaultConfiguration.level. Each diagnostic’s actual severity belongs in result.level.

The specification distinguishes:

Field | Meaning -- | -- rule.defaultConfiguration.level | The rule’s default severity; defaults to "warning" if omitted. result.level | The severity of this particular occurrence, overriding the rule default. invocation.ruleConfigurationOverrides | Optional recording of configuration changes for a run.

See SARIF §§3.49.14, 3.50.3, and 3.27.10. A rule can therefore default to "error" while individual results report "warning" because of per-file overrides.

The PR currently emits a different field: [`properties\["problem.severity"\]` (line 285)](/Users/micha/code/.worktrees/2e76/ruff/crates/ruff_db/src/diagnostic/render/sarif.rs:285). That is a GitHub convention, outside the standard severity mechanism. GitHub documents it separately, with values "error", "warning", and "recommendation". GitHub SARIF documentation.

For this implementation, I would:

  • Include the registry’s default severity in RuleMetadata and emit it as defaultConfiguration.level.
  • Continue emitting each diagnostic’s configured severity as result.level.
  • Remove the maximum-observed-severity calculation from the standard rule metadata path.

That also supports your earlier suggestion: the rule metadata can be prepared independently of the diagnostics. The specification does not require calculating its severity from the reported results.

One detail for ty: a default level of Ignore should be represented through defaultConfiguration.enabled: false; SARIF’s "none" severity does not mean “rule disabled.”

I'd be inclined to move `DisplayDiagnostics` into ruff/ty, as well as `DiagnosticFormat`.

I'm a bit hesitant to add more to `DiagnosticContext`. It's unclear if this will ever happen but ideally, Ruff would start using ty's `File`, which would then allow us to remove `FileResolver` and `DiagnosticContext`. But not if we add more. 

The other reason why I wouldn't add `RuleMetadataProvider` to `DiagnosticContext` is that we now make it available to all renderers, when only one renderer (Sarif) uses it. 

I think I'm leaning towards changing `SarifRenderer` to take a new `HashMap<LintName, RuleMetadata>` argument (or a newtype wrapper that stores all rule metadata. That seems simpler, and we also don't loose any laziness because the rule metadata is always emitted. 

The main downside of this is that we generate the metadata for all rules upfront. I suspect that this won't be too meaningful. 

If you think the lazyiness is important, I then suggest passing the rule metadata provider as a separate argument.

body:
Could we update the forwarded-parameter provenance to account for a later callback supplying the inferred signature?

```python
from typing import Callable

def forward[**P](
    left: Callable[P, None],
    right: Callable[P, None],
    /,
    *args: P.args,
    **kwargs: P.kwargs,
) -> None: ...

def broad(value: object, /) -> None: ...
def narrow(value: int, /) -> None: ...

forward(broad, narrow, "bad")
```

Inference now correctly chooses the narrower parameter list, but the "Expected `int`" diagnostic points to `broad`'s `value: object` declaration. `paramspec_parameter_source` still picks the first callback. Tracking the supplying signature, or falling back to the wrapper when it is ambiguous, would avoid that misleading annotation.

(I think this is the cause of the TODO at https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/29172/changes#diff-2238654f2794651442cc769c6bedf4e889f424f980bc9d81a3e7c977fb7df9a2R782 -- I guess it can also be left as a TODO, but might make sense to also have a TODO here about the fix?)

I think choosing one leaf here also replaces `P` inside prefix parameter annotations and nested return types. Those occurrences still need the full intersection. For example, this is accepted by the PR but rejected by main and all other type checkers, and raises `AttributeError` at runtime:

```python
from typing import Callable, Concatenate

def integer(callback: Callable[[int], None]) -> None:
    callback(1)

def text(callback: Callable[[str], None]) -> None:
    callback("s")

def only_int(x: int) -> None:
    print(x.bit_length())

def make[**P](
    left: Callable[[Callable[P, None]], None],
    right: Callable[[Callable[P, None]], None],
) -> Callable[Concatenate[Callable[P, None], P], None]:
    def wrapper(cb: Callable[P, None], /, *args: P.args, **kwargs: P.kwargs) -> None:
        left(cb)
        right(cb)
    return wrapper

make(integer, text)(only_int, 1)
```

The integer branch of the expanded return type accepts `only_int`, but `wrapper` passes it to both consumers, including `text`. The base rejects `make(integer, text)`.

Could we apply the leaf substitution only to the outer parameter-list splice, while specializing prefix annotations and return types with the original full binding? The same substitution also loses valid calls for a return type like `Callable[P, Callable[P, None]]`: calling the outer function with an integer incorrectly restricts the returned callback to integers.

Codex points out that the new fast path now makes equivalent cases behave differently depending whether the fast path is taken or not, because our slow path doesn't consistently implement "top accepts no calls" in this restricted receiver case. This new receiver test is accepted with a `str` return annotation (taking the fast path), but an equivalent alias or an unused generic parameter (taking the slow path) produces an `invalid-assignment`:

```python
from typing import Callable
from ty_extensions import Top

type Result = str

class Restricted:
    def ordinary(self: "Allowed") -> str:
        return ""

    def aliased(self: "Allowed") -> Result:
        return ""

    def generic[T](self: "Allowed") -> str:
        return ""

class Allowed(Restricted): ...

def check_receiver(restricted: Restricted) -> None:
    ordinary: Top[Callable[..., object]] = restricted.ordinary  # accepted
    aliased: Top[Callable[..., object]] = restricted.aliased  # invalid-assignment
    generic: Top[Callable[..., object]] = restricted.generic  # invalid-assignment
```

In the full signature check path, we check the unsatisfied receiver constraint before reaching the top-parameter shortcut. I would expect all three assignments to be accepted, while still retaining any inference bounds the fallback needs to collect.

I don't think this needs to block the PR: main rejects all three, so the remaining rejections are pre-existing. We could just record the inconsistency in a TODO comment for now.

+## Bottom callable assignability
+
+The bottom callable accepts every argument list and returns `Never`, so it can satisfy any callable
+signature, including one with required keyword-only parameters. Returning `Never` alone is not
+sufficient, nor is accepting every argument list with an incompatible return type.
+
+```py
+from typing import Any, Callable, Never, Protocol
+from ty_extensions import Bottom
+
+class Required(Protocol):
+    def __call__(self, value: int, /, *, enabled: bool) -> str: ...
+
+def never_returns(*values: object, **options: object) -> Never:
+    raise NotImplementedError
+
+def check(
+    bottom: Bottom[Callable[..., Any]],
+    restricted: Callable[[int], Never],
+    returns_none: Bottom[Callable[..., None]],
+) -> None:
+    positional: Callable[[str, bytes], int] = bottom  # no diagnostic
+    keyword_only: Required = bottom  # no diagnostic
+    declared: Required = never_returns  # no diagnostic
+
+    wrong_parameters: Callable[[str], int] = restricted  # error: [invalid-assignment]
+    wrong_return: Callable[[int], str] = returns_none  # error: [invalid-assignment]
+```
+
+Receiver restrictions still apply when a bound method accepts every argument list and returns
+`Never`.
+
+```py
+class Restricted:
+    def method(self: "Allowed", *values: object, **options: object) -> Never:
+        raise NotImplementedError
+
+class Allowed(Restricted): ...
+
+def check_receiver(restricted: Restricted, allowed: Allowed) -> None:
+    valid: Callable[[int], str] = allowed.method  # no diagnostic
+    invalid: Callable[[int], str] = restricted.method  # error: [invalid-assignment]
+```
+
+## Top callable assignability
+
+Every callable is assignable to the top callable, which permits no calls and has return type
+`object`. A narrower return type or a parameter list that permits calls still imposes requirements.
+
+```py
+from typing import Callable, Protocol
+from ty_extensions import Top
+
+class Required(Protocol):
+    def __call__(self, *, enabled: bool) -> bytes: ...
+
+def check(positional: Callable[[int], str], keyword_only: Required) -> None:
+    first: Top[Callable[..., object]] = positional  # no diagnostic
+    second: Top[Callable[..., object]] = keyword_only  # no diagnostic
+    wrong_return: Top[Callable[..., int]] = positional  # error: [invalid-assignment]
+    wrong_parameters: Top[Callable[[str], object]] = positional  # error: [invalid-assignment]
+```
+
+A receiver restriction does not prevent assignment to the top callable, since it permits no calls.
+The restriction still applies when assigning to a callable that permits calls.

+Consumers of different signatures produce a callback that supports calls using either signature.
+
+```py
+from typing import Concatenate
+
+def combine(left: Callable[[Callable[P, None]], None], right: Callable[[Callable[P, None]], None]) -> Callable[P, bytes]:
+    raise NotImplementedError
+
+def text(callback: Callable[[str], None]) -> None: ...
+def empty(callback: Callable[[], None]) -> None: ...
+
+callback = combine(consume, text)
+reveal_type(callback(1))  # revealed: bytes
+reveal_type(callback("text"))  # revealed: bytes
+# error: [invalid-argument-type]
+# error: [invalid-argument-type]
+callback(None)
+
+with_empty = combine(consume, empty)
+reveal_type(with_empty())  # revealed: bytes
+reveal_type(with_empty(1))  # revealed: bytes
+```
+
+A `ParamSpec` wrapper should preserve the combined callable's supported signatures.
+
+```py
+def preserve(callback: Callable[P, bytes]) -> Callable[P, bytes]:
+    return callback
+
+reveal_type(callback)  # revealed: ((int, /) -> bytes) & ((str, /) -> bytes)
+preserved = preserve(callback)
+# TODO: ((int, /) -> bytes) & ((str, /) -> bytes)
+reveal_type(preserved)  # revealed: (int, /) -> bytes
+preserved(1)
+# TODO: no error

body:
I think this PR weakens the precedence abstraction by using it to reclassify candidates based on it. I'd probably go and rename the struct and field if we want to use it as a kind instead. 


For example, we could have a `CanidateKind` or `Origin` with an `::sort_key(&self) -> impl Ord` method (similar to what we do for `Diagnostic`)

Could we preserve the inference evidence when taking this shortcut? `Never <= T` and `T <= object` are always satisfied, but the solver still uses these bounds to choose a specialization. Returning `self.always()` drops them and changes inferred types to `Unknown`:

```python
from typing import Callable, Never, reveal_type

def abort(*args: object, **kwargs: object) -> Never:
    raise RuntimeError

def wrap[T](f: Callable[[], T]) -> list[T]:
    return []

def wrap_param[T](f: Callable[[T], object]) -> list[T]:
    return []

reveal_type(wrap(abort))        # Base: list[Never]; PR: list[Unknown]
reveal_type(wrap_param(abort))  # Base: list[object]; PR: list[Unknown]
value: str = wrap_param(abort)[0]  # The invalid-assignment diagnostic disappears
```

The `target.is_top()` branch has the same problem in nested callable comparisons: a `T <= object` bound disappears, changing an inferred `object` to `Unknown`.

Could we restrict the shortcut to comparisons that don't need inference evidence, or retain the relevant bounds, and add regression coverage for both PEP 695 and legacy generics?
I think it should be as part of this PR because this PR now couples `package.json` and the CDN URL. I also don't think it adds much work. The main work is testing the playground.
Added, thanks!
